lessons.title: Databricks Runtime for ML and the compute it needs
lessons.summary: What the ML runtime gives you over the standard runtime, which access mode it requires, and where Photon and GPUs fit.

sections.heading: What the ML runtime is
sections.body:
**Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning (DBR ML)** creates compute with machine learning and deep learning infrastructure already built in. Common ML and DL libraries come **preinstalled and tested together**, so you do not spend time installing and pinning packages before you can train.

- Top-tier libraries are only added or removed with **major** runtime releases, which keeps environments stable across minor updates.
- MLflow, the Feature Engineering client and (on the runtimes that include it) AutoML are part of the experience.
- Because the library set is curated, a team that standardises on one ML runtime version gets reproducible environments across notebooks and jobs.

sections.heading: Turning it on: the Machine learning checkbox
sections.body:
In the create-compute UI you tick **Machine learning**. That selects an ML runtime and sets the access mode to **Dedicated** (formerly called *single user*).

| Access mode | Old name | ML notes |
|---|---|---|
| Dedicated | Single user | Required for Unity Catalog data access from the ML runtime; supports AutoML. Can be assigned to a user **or a group**. |
| Standard | Shared | Does **not** support AutoML. |

If someone reports that AutoML or UC access fails on their ML cluster, check the access mode first.

sections.heading: Photon, GPUs and version gates
sections.body:
- **Photon** is available on recent ML runtimes. It accelerates Spark SQL, DataFrames and feature engineering, but **not** single-node Python libraries such as XGBoost, PyTorch or TensorFlow training.
- Some features need a minimum ML runtime (for example, fine-grained access control and querying pipeline tables need a recent LTS ML runtime). Treat exact version numbers as fast-changing; the exam tests the idea that capabilities are gated by runtime version.
- For custom deep-learning GPU workloads Databricks now points to **AI Runtime**; DBR ML remains the classic-ML choice.

keyPoints: DBR ML = preinstalled, compatible ML/DL libraries plus MLflow integration.
The Machine learning checkbox selects an ML runtime and Dedicated access mode.
UC data access from DBR ML requires Dedicated access mode.
Standard (shared) access mode does not support AutoML.
Photon speeds up Spark workloads, not single-node Python training.

gotchas.trap: Photon makes every training job faster, including single-node PyTorch.
gotchas.correct: Photon accelerates Spark SQL/DataFrame work and feature engineering, not single-node Python libraries.

gotchas.trap: Any access mode works with AutoML.
gotchas.correct: AutoML is supported on Dedicated access mode, not on Standard (shared).

lessons.lab: Create a small compute resource with the Machine learning checkbox ticked. Note which access mode is selected, then run `import sklearn, mlflow; print(sklearn.__version__, mlflow.__version__)` without any `%pip install`.

lessons.title: AutoML: a glass-box starting point for model and feature selection
lessons.summary: What AutoML automates, which problem types and algorithms it covers, what it produces, and the compute and runtime constraints.

sections.heading: What AutoML does
sections.body:
AutoML takes a dataset and a target column and then:

1. **Prepares the data** for training.
2. Runs **distributed training and hyperparameter tuning across several algorithms**.
3. Logs **every trial as an MLflow run** with metrics and the model.
4. Generates a **source notebook for each trial**.

It is a **glass box**: instead of a black-box model, you get editable code. That is its main value in model development: a fast, reproducible baseline that shows which algorithms and features work, which you then refine.

sections.heading: Problem types and algorithms
sections.body:
| Problem type | Algorithms |
|---|---|
| Classification | Decision trees, random forests, logistic regression, XGBoost, LightGBM |
| Regression | Decision trees, random forests, linear regression with SGD, XGBoost, LightGBM |
| Forecasting | Prophet, Auto-ARIMA (serverless forecasting adds DeepAR) |

You can drive it from the **low-code UI** or the **Python API**.

sections.heading: What you get back
sections.body:
- **Data exploration notebook**: profiles the input so you can spot skew, missing values and suspicious columns. It helps with **feature selection**.
- **Best trial notebook**: the code that produced the best model, imported into the workspace automatically for classification and regression.
- Other trial notebooks are stored as **MLflow artifacts** and can be imported from the UI or with `databricks.automl.import_notebook`. For forecasting, all trial notebooks are imported.
- **SHAP** explainability code is included in trial notebooks but turned off by default; set `shap_enabled = True` to use it.

sections.heading: Constraints to remember
sections.body:
- Requires **Dedicated** access mode; Standard (shared) does not support AutoML.
- On the newest ML runtimes AutoML is **no longer a built-in library**; it depends on the `databricks-automl-runtime` package.
- Do not install extra libraries or change library versions on the cluster that runs AutoML, because that causes run failures.

keyPoints: AutoML = data prep + multi-algorithm tuning + one notebook per trial.
Every trial is an MLflow run; compare them in the experiment UI.
Classification, regression and forecasting are supported.
Data exploration and best-trial notebooks are imported automatically (classification/regression).
Glass box: you can edit and rerun the generated code.

gotchas.trap: AutoML returns only a model, so you cannot see how it was built.
gotchas.correct: AutoML generates a source notebook for each trial; it is a glass-box tool.

gotchas.trap: AutoML is a replacement for the data scientist.
gotchas.correct: It produces a baseline and code to customise; you still validate, refine and own the model.

lessons.lab: Run an AutoML classification experiment on a small UC table. Open the data exploration notebook, then compare the top three runs in the MLflow experiment and open the best trial notebook.

lessons.title: MLOps: promote code or promote models?
lessons.summary: The deploy-code, deploy-models and hybrid patterns, when each is right, and how Unity Catalog catalogs map to environments.

sections.heading: Two things can move between environments
sections.body:
An ML system has **code** (feature pipelines, training, inference, monitoring) and **models** (trained artifacts). MLOps on Databricks asks which one you promote through **dev, staging and prod**.

Typically each environment corresponds to a **catalog in Unity Catalog** (for example `dev`, `staging`, `prod`), so access control follows the environment.

sections.heading: Deploy code (recommended in most situations)
sections.body:
Training **code** is developed in dev, reviewed and tested in staging (training on a subset of data), then deployed to prod, where the model is **retrained on full production data**.

- **Pros:** retraining in prod is safe because the code was reviewed; **production data can stay in prod**; automated retraining is natural.
- **Con:** data scientists face a steeper learning curve handing code to CI/CD.

sections.heading: Deploy models
Hybrid and MLOps habits
sections.body:
**Hybrid:** deploy code to staging, train there, then deploy the resulting model to prod.

Good habits regardless of pattern: version code in Git, track every training run in MLflow, register models in UC with signatures, use aliases for promotion, and automate tests between environments.

keyPoints: Deploy code is the default recommendation.
Deploy models fits expensive one-off training, single workspace, or no CI/CD.
Deploy code keeps prod data in prod and makes retraining natural.
Environments typically map to UC catalogs.
Hybrid: code to staging, train there, model to prod.

gotchas.trap: Deploying models is always simpler and therefore best practice.
gotchas.correct: Databricks recommends deploying code in most situations; deploy models is for specific constraints.

gotchas.trap: With deploy models, only the model needs to reach prod.
gotchas.correct: Feature, inference and monitoring code must still be deployed to prod separately.

lessons.lab: Sketch three catalogs (dev, staging, prod) for a churn project. For each pattern, write down where training runs, where the model is registered and which data each environment reads.

lessons.title: Feature tables in Unity Catalog: create and write
lessons.summary: How a UC feature table is defined, the FeatureEngineeringClient calls to create and write one, and how to convert an existing Delta table.

sections.heading: A feature table is a Delta table with a primary key
sections.body:
In Unity Catalog, **any Delta table with a primary key constraint is a feature table**. That is the whole definition, and it is why UC feature tables get UC governance, lineage and discovery for free.

Requirements: a UC-enabled workspace and a recent runtime. The `databricks-feature-engineering` client is included in DBR ML (13.3 LTS ML and above); elsewhere run `%pip install databricks-feature-engineering`.

sections.heading: Create with the client
sections.body:
```python
from databricks.feature_engineering import FeatureEngineeringClient
fe = FeatureEngineeringClient()

fe.create_table(
    name="ml.features.customer_features",   # catalog.schema.table
    primary_keys=["customer_id"],             # list for composite keys
    df=features_df,                           # or schema=features_df.schema
    timeseries_columns="snapshot_date",       # optional
    description="Customer aggregates",
)
```

- Passing `df` creates the table and writes the data; passing `schema` creates an empty table.
- `timeseries_columns` marks a timestamp key so training can do **point-in-time** lookups.

sections.heading: Convert an existing table with SQL
Write and delete
sections.body:
```python
fe.write_table(name="ml.features.customer_features", df=updates_df, mode="merge")
```

- `mode="merge"` upserts by primary key. **Rows whose keys are not in `updates_df` stay unchanged.**
- `fe.drop_table(name=...)` or `DROP TABLE` removes the feature table and the underlying Delta table.

keyPoints: UC feature table = Delta table with a primary key constraint.
Create with fe.create_table(name, primary_keys, df or schema, timeseries_columns).
Convert existing tables with ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... PRIMARY KEY.
PK columns must be NOT NULL.
fe.write_table(mode="merge") upserts and leaves other rows untouched.

gotchas.trap: Use ALTER TABLE ... SET AS FEATURE STORE to register a table.
gotchas.correct: No such clause exists; adding a primary key constraint makes it a feature table.

gotchas.trap: write_table in merge mode deletes rows not present in the new DataFrame.
gotchas.correct: Merge upserts by key; rows absent from the DataFrame are unchanged.

lessons.title: Training and scoring with feature tables
lessons.summary: FeatureLookup and create_training_set for training, fe.log_model to package lookup metadata, and score_batch for inference.

sections.heading: Build a training set
sections.body:
Start from a DataFrame with **lookup keys and the label** only. Features are joined from feature tables:

```python
from databricks.feature_engineering import FeatureLookup

lookups = [
  FeatureLookup(table_name="ml.features.customer_features",
                feature_names=["tenure", "avg_spend"],
                lookup_key="customer_id",
                timestamp_lookup_key="event_ts"),   # point-in-time
]
training_set = fe.create_training_set(df=labels_df, feature_lookups=lookups,
                                      label="churned", exclude_columns=["customer_id"])
train_df = training_set.load_df()
```

`timestamp_lookup_key` gives a **point-in-time join** against a time-series feature table, which avoids leaking future values into training.

sections.heading: Log the model with the Feature Engineering client
sections.body:
```python
fe.log_model(model=model, artifact_path="model", flavor=mlflow.sklearn,
             training_set=training_set,
             registered_model_name="ml.models.churn")
```

You **must** log with `FeatureEngineeringClient.log_model` for automatic lookup at inference. It packages the **feature lookup metadata** with the model. Logging with plain `mlflow.sklearn.log_model` loses that metadata.

sections.heading: Score in batch
sections.body:
```python
preds = fe.score_batch(model_uri="models:/ml.models.churn@Champion", df=keys_df)
```

- `keys_df` needs only the lookup keys; features are **looked up automatically**.
- If `keys_df` already contains a feature column, **the provided value overrides the lookup**.
- Missing features come back as NaN.
- For real-time serving, Model Serving looks up features that were **published to an online store** automatically.

Limit to know conceptually: a model can use a bounded number of feature tables and functions.

keyPoints: Labels DataFrame + FeatureLookup list -> fe.create_training_set -> load_df().
timestamp_lookup_key enables point-in-time correctness.
Log with fe.log_model(training_set=...) to embed lookup metadata.
fe.score_batch needs only keys; passed-in columns override lookups.
Model Serving uses online stores for automatic real-time lookup.

gotchas.trap: Logging with mlflow.sklearn.log_model is enough for score_batch to find features.
gotchas.correct: Use fe.log_model with the training_set so feature metadata is packaged with the model.

gotchas.trap: score_batch requires you to join all features yourself first.
gotchas.correct: score_batch looks up features from keys automatically.

lessons.title: Account-level vs workspace features, and online vs offline stores
lessons.summary: Why UC feature tables beat the deprecated Workspace Feature Store, and how offline Delta tables relate to Lakebase-backed Online Feature Stores.

sections.heading: Account-level (UC) vs workspace-level
sections.body:
Feature tables in Unity Catalog live in the account-level metastore. Benefits over the workspace-scoped **Workspace Feature Store** (now **deprecated**, only for workspaces without UC):

- **Sharing across workspaces** attached to the same metastore, with no copying.
- **Centralised governance**: UC privileges on catalogs, schemas and tables.
- **Lineage** from features to the models that use them.
- **Discovery** of features in Catalog Explorer alongside other UC assets.

sections.heading: Offline tables
sections.body: The **offline** feature table is the UC Delta table. It is the **source of truth**, used for **training and batch scoring**, and can hold full history.

sections.heading: Online stores
sections.body:
An **online store** is a **low-latency copy** of feature values for **real-time serving**. On Databricks this is now **Databricks Online Feature Stores, powered by Lakebase**:

```python
fe.create_online_store(name="churn-online", capacity="CU_1")
fe.publish_table(...)   # source UC feature table -> online store, publish_mode="TRIGGERED"
```

- Publish modes: **TRIGGERED** (default), **CONTINUOUS**, **SNAPSHOT**.
- Publishing needs a primary key with non-null columns, and **Change Data Feed** on the source for TRIGGERED and CONTINUOUS.
- By default only the **latest value per key** is published.
- Only UC feature tables can be published. The older "online tables" product is retired.

sections.heading: Feature Views (current recommendation)
sections.body: For new use cases Databricks now recommends **Feature Views**, declarative features whose pipelines Databricks manages. Feature tables remain supported. Exam objectives are written around feature tables, so know those first.

keyPoints: UC feature tables are shared across workspaces on the same metastore.
Workspace Feature Store is deprecated.
Offline = Delta source of truth for training and batch.
Online = low-latency copy for real-time serving (Lakebase).
Publish modes: TRIGGERED, CONTINUOUS, SNAPSHOT; CDF needed for the first two.

gotchas.trap: Train models directly from the online store for consistency.
gotchas.correct: Training and batch scoring read the offline Delta table; the online store serves low-latency lookups.

gotchas.trap: Each workspace needs its own copy of a UC feature table.
gotchas.correct: UC feature tables are account-level and accessible from any workspace on the same metastore.

lessons.title: MLflow tracking: manual logging, the UI and finding the best run
lessons.summary: Logging params, metrics, artifacts and models by hand, what the MLflow UI shows, searching runs with the Client API, and MLflow 3 changes.

sections.heading: Manual logging inside a run
sections.body:
```python
import mlflow
with mlflow.start_run(run_name="rf-depth-8"):
    mlflow.log_params({"max_depth": 8, "n_estimators": 300})
    mlflow.log_metric("val_auc", auc)
    mlflow.log_artifact("confusion_matrix.png")   # any local file
    mlflow.log_figure(fig, "roc.png")              # matplotlib figure
    mlflow.log_dict(cfg, "config.json")
    mlflow.set_tag("team", "growth")
    mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, name="model", input_example=X_val[:5])
```

- **Params** are inputs (hyperparameters). **Metrics** are numeric results and can be logged per step. **Artifacts** are files. **Tags** are free-form labels.
- Passing `input_example` (or using autologging) records a **model signature**, which UC registration requires.

sections.heading: MLflow 3 changes you will see
sections.body:
- `log_model(..., name="model")` replaces `artifact_path=` (still accepted, deprecated).
- Models are first-class **LoggedModel** entities with an ID, addressed as `models:/<model_id>`; a run is no longer strictly required to log a model.
- The default registry URI is `databricks-uc`.
- `mlflow.evaluate` is deprecated in favour of `mlflow.models.evaluate`; `run_uuid` is removed in favour of `run_id`.

sections.heading: Finding the best run
sections.body:
```python
from mlflow import MlflowClient
client = MlflowClient()
best = client.search_runs(
    experiment_ids=[exp_id],
    filter_string="params.model_type = 'xgboost'",
    order_by=["metrics.val_mae ASC"],
    max_results=1,
)[0]
print(best.info.run_id, best.data.metrics["val_mae"])
```

- Order **ASC** for error metrics (lower is better), **DESC** for scores like AUC or F1.
- `mlflow.search_runs(...)` takes similar arguments and returns a **pandas DataFrame**.

sections.heading: What the MLflow UI shows
sections.body: For each run: **parameters, metrics (with charts), tags, artifacts** (including the logged model and its signature, and the notebook for AutoML trials), the **source notebook and revision**, start time, duration and user. You can **compare runs** side by side and see **parent and child runs** created by hyperparameter tuning.

keyPoints: log_param(s), log_metric(s), log_artifact, log_figure, log_dict, set_tag, <flavor>.log_model.
Signature via input_example or autologging; UC needs it.
search_runs with order_by and max_results=1 finds the best run.
ASC for errors, DESC for scores.
MLflow 3: name= replaces artifact_path=; LoggedModel IDs.

gotchas.trap: Sort by metrics.rmse DESC to find the best regression run.
gotchas.correct: Lower RMSE is better, so sort ASC.

gotchas.trap: Hyperparameters should be logged with log_metric.
gotchas.correct: Inputs are params (log_param); metrics are measured results.

lessons.title: Models in Unity Catalog: register, tag and promote with aliases
lessons.summary: Registering models in UC, privileges, tags at model and version level, champion/challenger aliases, and why UC beats the legacy workspace registry.

sections.heading: Registering
sections.body:
```python
mlflow.set_registry_uri("databricks-uc")   # default in MLflow 3
mlflow.register_model(model_uri, "ml.models.churn")
# or log_model(..., registered_model_name="ml.models.churn")
# or MlflowClient().create_registered_model / create_model_version
```

- Names are three-level: `<catalog>.<schema>.<model>`.
- Privileges: **USE CATALOG**, **USE SCHEMA** and **CREATE MODEL** on the schema.
- **New model versions in UC must have a model signature.**

sections.heading: Aliases replace stages
sections.body:
UC does **not support stages** (None/Staging/Production/Archived). Use **aliases**: mutable, named pointers to one version.

```python
client.set_registered_model_alias("ml.models.churn", "Challenger", 7)
client.get_model_version_by_alias("ml.models.churn", "Champion")
client.delete_registered_model_alias("ml.models.churn", "Challenger")
model = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("models:/ml.models.churn@Champion")
```

- Only **one version holds a given alias** at a time; setting it on a new version moves it.
- **Promoting challenger to champion** = set the `Champion` alias on the challenger's version number. Consumers loading `@Champion` pick up the new version without code changes.

sections.heading: Tags
sections.body:
| Scope | Set | Remove |
|---|---|---|
| Registered model | `set_registered_model_tag` | `delete_registered_model_tag` |
| Model version | `set_model_version_tag` | `delete_model_version_tag` |

Setting tags requires ownership or the `APPLY TAG` privilege. Use version tags for facts about one version (for example `validation_status=passed`).

sections.heading: UC registry vs workspace registry
sections.body:
Benefits of Models in UC:

- **Centralised governance** and ACLs across workspaces.
- Access from **any workspace on the same metastore**.
- **Lineage** from models back to upstream tables.
- Sharing across regions and accounts with Delta Sharing.
- Environments as catalogs; cross-environment promotion with `copy_model_version`.

The **Workspace Model Registry** is legacy: it uses stages via `transition_model_version_stage`, and stage APIs such as `get_latest_versions` are deprecated in MLflow. Know the UC limits too: no registry webhooks, and deletion is irreversible.

keyPoints: Three-level names; set_registry_uri("databricks-uc") (default in MLflow 3).
Signature required for new UC versions.
Aliases, not stages; one version per alias.
Promote = move Champion alias to the challenger version.
Model tags vs version tags have separate set/delete methods.

gotchas.trap: Call transition_model_version_stage(..., "Production") on a UC model.
gotchas.correct: Stages are not supported in UC; set the Champion alias instead.

gotchas.trap: An alias can point to several versions for A/B testing.
gotchas.correct: Each alias points to exactly one version; use two aliases (Champion, Challenger).

lessons.title: Summarising and visualising features on Databricks
lessons.summary: Profile a Spark DataFrame with describe(), summary() and dbutils.data.summarize, then pick the right chart or statistic to inspect one feature or compare two.

sections.heading: Why profile before you model
sections.body: Section 2 of the exam guide starts with exploratory analysis: compute summary statistics on a Spark DataFrame, visualise categorical and continuous features, and compare pairs of features. Profiling tells you which columns have **missing values**, **skew**, **outliers** or **very many categories**, and those findings drive every later choice in this domain (imputation strategy, outlier rule, encoding and log transforms).

sections.heading: describe() vs summary()
sections.body:
Both are PySpark `DataFrame` methods that return a new DataFrame of statistics.

| Method | Default statistics |
|---|---|
| `df.describe()` | count, mean, stddev, min, max |
| `df.summary()` | count, mean, stddev, min, **25%, 50%, 75%**, max |

`summary()` adds the quartiles, which is what you need for the IQR outlier rule. You can also ask for specific statistics, for example `df.summary("count", "min", "10%", "90%", "max")`. The percentiles are **approximate**, computed with an approximate quantile algorithm, so do not treat them as exact on large data.

Both return string-typed result columns; use `.show()` or `display()` to view them. String columns get count, min and max but no mean.

sections.heading: dbutils.data.summarize
sections.body:
`dbutils.data.summarize(df, precise=False)` computes and **displays** summary statistics for a Spark or pandas DataFrame in a notebook, including histograms and per-column profiles. Key behaviour from the Databricks Utilities docs:

- It scans the whole DataFrame.
- By default (`precise=False`) results are **approximate**: distinct counts on high-cardinality columns can be off by about 5%, and histograms and percentiles by a very small amount.
- `precise=True` makes everything exact **except** histograms and percentiles, which become far more accurate but are still approximate.

The notebook `display()` output also offers a **Data Profile** tab that shows the same kind of profile without code, and built-in chart types.

sections.heading: Choosing a visual or statistic
sections.body:
| What you are looking at | Good choice |
|---|---|
| One continuous feature | Histogram, density plot, box plot |
| One categorical feature | Bar chart or count plot of category frequencies |
| Two continuous features | Scatter plot; Pearson correlation (linear) or Spearman (monotonic, rank-based) |
| Two categorical features | Contingency table (cross-tab), stacked bar chart, chi-square test of independence |
| Continuous vs categorical | Grouped (side-by-side) box plots |

In Spark ML, `pyspark.ml.stat.Correlation.corr` computes Pearson or Spearman correlation matrices over a vector column, and `ChiSquareTest` tests independence between categorical features and a label. For quick checks, `df.stat.corr(col1, col2)` and `df.crosstab(col1, col2)` work on DataFrame columns.

keyPoints: summary() = describe() plus 25%, 50% and 75% approximate percentiles.
dbutils.data.summarize is approximate by default; precise=True makes counts exact but percentiles and histograms stay approximate.
Pearson measures linear association; Spearman measures monotonic association on ranks and is less sensitive to outliers.
Two categorical features: contingency table plus chi-square, not a correlation coefficient.
Continuous vs categorical: grouped box plots.

gotchas.trap: describe() gives you the median and quartiles.
gotchas.correct: describe() gives count, mean, stddev, min and max only. Use summary() for quartiles.

gotchas.trap: precise=True in dbutils.data.summarize makes every statistic exact.
gotchas.correct: Histograms and percentiles remain approximate even with precise=True; only the error shrinks.

gotchas.correct: Use a cross-tab and a chi-square test for two categorical features.

lessons.title: Detecting and removing outliers in Spark
lessons.summary: Filter outliers with the standard-deviation rule or the IQR rule using Spark aggregations and approxQuantile, and know when each rule fits the data.

sections.heading: Two rules the exam expects
sections.body:
**Standard-deviation (z-score) rule.** Keep rows where the value lies within `mean ± k·stddev`. A common choice is k = 3. It assumes a roughly symmetric, bell-shaped distribution, and the outliers themselves inflate the mean and standard deviation, so extreme values can hide the very points you want to remove.

**IQR rule.** Compute the first and third quartiles, Q1 and Q3, and IQR = Q3 − Q1. Keep rows inside `[Q1 − 1.5·IQR, Q3 + 1.5·IQR]`. Quartiles barely move when a few extreme values appear, so the IQR rule is **robust** and works better for skewed data. These are general statistics conventions rather than Databricks features.

sections.heading: Standard deviation rule in PySpark
sections.body:
```python
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
stats = df.select(F.mean("amount").alias("mu"), F.stddev("amount").alias("sd")).first()
lo, hi = stats.mu - 3 * stats.sd, stats.mu + 3 * stats.sd
clean = df.filter(F.col("amount").between(lo, hi))
```

Compute the statistics once on the training data and reuse the same bounds on validation and scoring data, so the rule does not leak information from the evaluation set.

sections.heading: IQR rule in PySpark
sections.body:
```python
q1, q3 = df.approxQuantile("amount", [0.25, 0.75], 0.01)
iqr = q3 - q1
clean = df.filter(F.col("amount").between(q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr))
```

`approxQuantile(col, probabilities, relativeError)` returns approximate quantiles; `relativeError = 0` computes exact quantiles but can be expensive on large data. In SQL, `percentile_approx(col, array(0.25, 0.75))` does the same job. `df.summary()` also shows the 25% and 75% values if you just want to inspect them.

sections.heading: Remove, cap or keep?
sections.body:
- **Remove** rows that are clearly data errors (negative ages, sensor glitches).
- **Cap (winsorise)** to the bounds when the extreme values are real but you want to limit their influence on mean-based models.
- **Keep** genuine extremes when they are the signal, for example in fraud or anomaly detection. Dropping them would delete the positive class.
- Never remove outliers from the **label** of the test set just to make metrics look better.

Always check how many rows a rule drops before and after, with `df.count()` and `clean.count()`.

keyPoints: Std-dev rule: keep mean ± k·σ (often k = 3); sensitive to skew and to the outliers themselves.
IQR rule: keep [Q1 − 1.5·IQR, Q3 + 1.5·IQR]; robust and preferred for skewed data.
df.approxQuantile(col, [0.25, 0.75], relErr) gets quartiles; relErr = 0 is exact but costly.
Fit bounds on training data, then apply the same bounds everywhere.
In anomaly or fraud use cases, extremes may be the signal, so do not blindly drop them.

gotchas.trap: The z-score rule is the safest choice for a heavily right-skewed column.
gotchas.correct: Skew inflates σ and distorts the bounds; the IQR rule or a log transform first is more appropriate.

gotchas.trap: Recompute outlier bounds separately on the test set.
gotchas.correct: Compute bounds on training data and apply them unchanged to test and scoring data.

lessons.lab: Pick a skewed numeric column. Compute bounds with both the 3σ rule and the 1.5·IQR rule, count how many rows each removes, and plot histograms of the result. Repeat after applying `F.log1p` to the column and compare how the two rules behave.

lessons.title: Imputing missing values: mean, median or mode
lessons.summary: Choose an imputation strategy from the column type and distribution, apply it with Spark ML Imputer inside a pipeline, and avoid leakage.

sections.heading: Pick the strategy from the distribution
sections.body:
| Strategy | Use for | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| **Mean** | Continuous, roughly symmetric data without strong outliers | Pulled toward extreme values and skew |
| **Median** | Continuous data that is **skewed** or has outliers | Ignores the shape of the tails |
| **Mode** (most frequent) | **Categorical** or discrete data | Can over-represent the dominant category |

No imputer chooses for you: you must inspect the distribution (for example with `summary()` or a histogram) and pick a strategy. When missingness itself may be informative, add an **indicator column** such as `income_was_missing` before imputing.

sections.heading: Spark ML Imputer
sections.body:
```python
from pyspark.ml.feature import Imputer
imp = Imputer(strategy="median", inputCols=["income", "age"], outputCols=["income_imp", "age_imp"])
model = imp.fit(train_df)      # Imputer is an Estimator
train_out = model.transform(train_df)
test_out = model.transform(test_df)
```

- `strategy` accepts `"mean"` (default), `"median"` or `"mode"`.
- It works on **numeric** columns. Null values and the configured `missingValue` (default NaN) are treated as missing.
- The Spark docs warn that Imputer does not support categorical features and can create incorrect values for them. For string categoricals, fill with the most frequent value (for example `df.fillna({"city": top_city})`) or index them first.
- Because `fit()` learns the fill value, put Imputer in a `Pipeline` and fit it on **training data only**, so test data does not leak into the statistic.

sections.heading: Drop or impute?
sections.body:
Dropping rows (`df.na.drop()`) is acceptable when very few rows are affected and the data is missing at random. Dropping many rows shrinks the training set and can bias it. Dropping a whole column makes sense when most of its values are missing and it carries little signal.

Some tree-based libraries can handle missing values natively, but for Spark ML linear models and most transformers you need to impute first, because NaN or null values break the vector assembly step or the training.

keyPoints: Mean for symmetric continuous data; median for skewed or outlier-heavy data; mode for categorical data.
Spark ML Imputer: strategy mean (default), median or mode; numeric inputs only.
Imputer is an Estimator: fit on training data, transform train and test with the fitted model.
Add a missing-indicator column when missingness may carry signal.

gotchas.trap: Use mean imputation on income data with a long right tail.
gotchas.correct: The tail drags the mean upward; median imputation is the robust choice.

gotchas.trap: Run Imputer on a string category column with strategy="mode".
gotchas.correct: Imputer is for numeric columns; fill string categoricals with the most frequent value or index them first.

gotchas.trap: Fit the imputer on the full dataset before splitting.
gotchas.correct: Split first, then fit on training data to avoid leakage.

lessons.lab: Create a DataFrame with a skewed numeric column containing nulls. Fit Imputer with strategy="mean" and strategy="median" on a training split, compare the learned fill values, and plot the distributions after each. Then add an indicator column and build a Pipeline of Imputer, VectorAssembler and LinearRegression.

lessons.title: One-hot encoding and log transforms
lessons.summary: Encode categorical features with StringIndexer and OneHotEncoder when the model needs it, know when not to one-hot encode, and use log transforms for skewed positive data.

sections.heading: One-hot encoding in Spark ML
sections.body:
Spark ML needs numeric vectors, so string categories go through two stages:

```python
from pyspark.ml.feature import StringIndexer, OneHotEncoder, VectorAssembler
idx = StringIndexer(inputCols=["plan", "region"], outputCols=["plan_idx", "region_idx"], handleInvalid="keep")
ohe = OneHotEncoder(inputCols=["plan_idx", "region_idx"], outputCols=["plan_ohe", "region_ohe"])
va  = VectorAssembler(inputCols=["plan_ohe", "region_ohe", "tenure"], outputCol="features")
```

- `StringIndexer` maps each label to an index, by default ordered by **frequency** (most frequent gets 0).
- `OneHotEncoder` is an **Estimator** in current Spark: it learns the category sizes during `fit()`. It outputs **sparse vectors** and by default drops the last category (`dropLast=True`) so the columns are not perfectly collinear.
- `handleInvalid` controls what happens to categories not seen during fitting (`"error"`, `"keep"` or `"skip"` depending on the stage).

sections.heading: When one-hot encoding fits, and when it does not
sections.body:
**Good fit:** nominal (unordered) categorical features with **low cardinality** feeding **linear models**, logistic regression or **distance-based** models, which would otherwise read an index as a meaningful number.

**Poor fit:**

- **High-cardinality** features (thousands of zip codes or product IDs): OHE creates a huge, sparse feature space. Consider grouping rare levels, target or frequency encoding, hashing, or embeddings.
- **Tree-based models** (decision trees, random forests, gradient-boosted trees): they can split on indexed categories directly, and in Spark ML they can treat a StringIndexer output as categorical through column metadata. OHE spreads one feature across many sparse columns, so trees grow deeper and each split sees less signal.
- **Ordinal** features (small < medium < large): an ordered index keeps the ordering that OHE throws away.

sections.heading: Log transforms
sections.body:
Apply a log transform to **right-skewed, positive** values that span orders of magnitude, such as prices, incomes, counts or durations. It compresses the long tail, makes the distribution closer to symmetric, reduces the leverage of extreme values and often makes relationships more linear.

- Use `F.log1p(col)` (log(1 + x)) when the column contains **zeros**; plain `log(0)` is undefined.
- It is **undefined for negative values**, so shift or choose another transform for signed data.
- If you transform the **target**, the model predicts in log space. Apply `exp` (or `expm1` after `log1p`) to predictions **before** computing RMSE or MAE in the original units or reporting results.
- A log transform does nothing useful for categorical codes, roughly symmetric features or features already on a narrow range.

keyPoints: StringIndexer then OneHotEncoder then VectorAssembler; OneHotEncoder is an Estimator with sparse output and dropLast=True by default.
OHE suits low-cardinality nominal features for linear and distance-based models.
Avoid OHE for high-cardinality features and usually for tree-based models; keep ordinal features as ordered indexes.
Log transform right-skewed positive data; log1p handles zeros; negatives are undefined.
Exponentiate predictions of a log-target model before computing metrics in original units.

gotchas.trap: Feed StringIndexer output straight into a linear regression as a numeric feature.
gotchas.correct: A linear model reads the index as an ordered magnitude; one-hot encode nominal features first.

gotchas.trap: One-hot encode a 40,000-level product ID for a random forest.
gotchas.correct: That explodes dimensionality and weakens tree splits; use indexing, grouping or another encoding.

gotchas.trap: Compute RMSE directly on log-space predictions against raw targets.
gotchas.correct: Convert predictions back with exp or expm1 first so both are in the same units.

Compare feature vector sizes and training time. Then log1p-transform a skewed numeric column, plot before-and-after histograms, and confirm that expm1 returns the original values.

lessons.title: Choosing an algorithm and handling class imbalance
lessons.summary: How to map a business problem to a model family, why a simple baseline comes first, and the main ways to deal with a rare positive class without fooling yourself with accuracy.

sections.heading: Start from the target, not the algorithm
sections.body:
Pick the problem type from the label first:

- **Categorical label** (churn yes/no, fraud class, product category): **classification**.
- **Continuous label** (revenue, duration, price): **regression**.
- **Label indexed by time where you predict future values**: **forecasting**.
- **No label at all** (group customers by behaviour): **unsupervised**, such as clustering.

Databricks AutoML mirrors this split: it supports classification, regression and forecasting, and for classification it tries decision trees, random forests, logistic regression, XGBoost and LightGBM. That list is a good mental shortlist for tabular data on the exam.

sections.heading: Trade-offs between model families
sections.body:
- **Linear and logistic regression**: fast, interpretable coefficients, a strong baseline. They assume a roughly linear relationship, are sensitive to feature scale when regularised, and need categorical features encoded (for example one-hot).
- **Decision trees**: interpretable rules and capture non-linearity, but a single deep tree overfits easily.
- **Random forests** (bagging of trees): reduce variance compared with a single tree; robust default for tabular data; little scaling or encoding effort (Spark tree models can use indexed categoricals directly).
- **Gradient-boosted trees** (GBT, XGBoost, LightGBM): often the most accurate on tabular data, but more hyperparameters and easier to overfit if not tuned.

A sensible workflow: train a simple baseline, then a tree ensemble, and compare them on the **same validation data and metric**. Prefer the simpler model when the gain is negligible, especially when stakeholders need explanations.

sections.heading: Class imbalance
sections.body:
When one class is rare (for example 2% fraud), a model that always predicts the majority class scores 98% accuracy and is useless. Mitigations:

- **Choose the right metric**: precision, recall, F1 or PR-AUC instead of accuracy.
- **Weight the classes (cost-sensitive learning)**: Spark ML classifiers such as `LogisticRegression` accept a `weightCol`; scikit-learn models accept `class_weight`. Errors on the rare class then cost more during training.
- **Resample the training data**: oversample the minority class, undersample the majority, or generate synthetic minority examples (SMOTE).
- **Stratify splits** so validation data has the same class ratio as production.
- **Tune the decision threshold** on validation data instead of using 0.5 blindly.

Resample **only the training split**. Oversampling before the split leaks duplicated rows into validation and inflates the score.

keyPoints: Label type decides the problem: categorical → classification, continuous → regression, future values over time → forecasting, no label → unsupervised.
Start with an interpretable baseline, then try tree ensembles, and compare on the same validation metric.
Tree ensembles handle non-linearity and interactions with little feature scaling; linear models need encoding and benefit from scaling when regularised.
For imbalance, change the metric and use class weights or resampling; never trust accuracy alone.
Resample after splitting, and only the training data.

gotchas.trap: A 97% accurate fraud model must be good.
gotchas.correct: With 3% positives, predicting "not fraud" every time gives 97% accuracy. Check recall, precision, F1 or PR-AUC.

gotchas.trap: Oversample the whole dataset, then split into train and validation.
gotchas.correct: Split first, then resample only the training split, or the validation set contains copies of training rows.

gotchas.trap: The most complex model is always the right choice.
gotchas.correct: Prefer the simplest model that meets the requirement; extra complexity raises variance and lowers interpretability.

lessons.lab: In a Databricks notebook, train a Spark ML LogisticRegression on an imbalanced binary dataset twice: once plain, once with a weightCol giving the minority class a weight equal to the class ratio. Compare accuracy, areaUnderPR and recall for the minority class.

lessons.title: Spark ML transformers, estimators and pipelines
lessons.summary: The Spark ML abstractions the exam uses: what a Transformer and an Estimator are, how a Pipeline becomes a PipelineModel, and how to build a reusable training pipeline.

sections.heading: Transformer vs Estimator
sections.body:
- A **Transformer** implements `transform()`: it takes a DataFrame and returns a new DataFrame, usually with appended columns. Examples: `VectorAssembler`, `Tokenizer`, and every fitted model.
- An **Estimator** implements `fit()`: it learns from a DataFrame and returns a **Model**, which is itself a Transformer. Examples: `LogisticRegression` (fits to `LogisticRegressionModel`), `StringIndexer` (learns the label-to-index mapping), `StandardScaler` (learns means and standard deviations), `Imputer`.

Rule of thumb: if the step must **learn something from data** (a vocabulary, a statistic, weights), it is an Estimator. If it is a fixed, stateless operation, it is a Transformer.

sections.heading: Pipelines
sections.body:
A **Pipeline** chains stages in order and is itself an **Estimator**.

```python
from pyspark.ml import Pipeline
from pyspark.ml.feature import StringIndexer, OneHotEncoder, VectorAssembler
from pyspark.ml.classification import LogisticRegression

idx = StringIndexer(inputCol="plan", outputCol="plan_idx")
ohe = OneHotEncoder(inputCols=["plan_idx"], outputCols=["plan_ohe"])
vec = VectorAssembler(inputCols=["plan_ohe", "tenure", "spend"], outputCol="features")
lr  = LogisticRegression(featuresCol="features", labelCol="label")

pipeline = Pipeline(stages=[idx, ohe, vec, lr])
model = pipeline.fit(train_df)          # PipelineModel
preds = model.transform(test_df)
```

- `pipeline.fit()` runs the stages in order: Transformers transform, Estimators are fit and their models then transform the data for the next stage.
- The result is a **PipelineModel**, a Transformer with the same number of stages, all now transformers.
- Each stage must be a **unique instance**; reusing the same object twice in one pipeline is not allowed.

sections.heading: Why pipelines matter
sections.body:
- **No leakage**: statistics such as imputation values or scaling parameters are learned from training data only, then reused on test and production data.
- **Consistency**: the exact same preprocessing runs at training and inference time, because you save and log one PipelineModel.
- **Tuning**: a whole Pipeline can be passed as the `estimator` to `CrossValidator` or `TrainValidationSplit`, so preprocessing is refit inside each fold.
- Parameters can be set with setters or passed in a `ParamMap`; values in a ParamMap override those set with setters.

keyPoints: Transformer = transform(): DataFrame in, DataFrame out.
Estimator = fit(): learns from data and returns a Model, which is a Transformer.
A Pipeline is an Estimator; Pipeline.fit() returns a PipelineModel, which is a Transformer.
StringIndexer, StandardScaler, Imputer and learning algorithms are Estimators; VectorAssembler and fitted models are Transformers.
Fit the pipeline on training data only, and pass the whole pipeline into the tuner to avoid leakage.

gotchas.trap: StringIndexer is a Transformer because it only converts strings to numbers.
gotchas.correct: It must learn the category-to-index mapping from data, so it is an Estimator that produces a StringIndexerModel.

gotchas.trap: A fitted PipelineModel still needs fit() before scoring new data.
gotchas.correct: A PipelineModel is a Transformer; call transform() on new data.

gotchas.trap: Fit the scaler on the full dataset, then split.
gotchas.correct: Fit preprocessing on training data only, ideally inside a Pipeline, so validation data stays unseen.

lessons.lab: Build a Pipeline with StringIndexer, OneHotEncoder, VectorAssembler and a RandomForestClassifier. Fit it on a training split, print model.stages to see each fitted stage type, then call transform() on the test split.

lessons.title: Search strategies and Hyperopt fmin with SparkTrials
lessons.summary: Grid, random and Bayesian search compared, then the Hyperopt API the exam still tests: fmin, search spaces, TPE vs random, and SparkTrials vs Trials for parallel tuning.

sections.heading: Grid, random and Bayesian search
sections.body:
- **Grid search** tries every combination in a discrete grid. Simple and reproducible, but the number of runs multiplies with each hyperparameter, and it wastes runs on unimportant dimensions.
- **Random search** samples combinations from distributions. For the same budget it usually explores important hyperparameters better than a grid, especially in higher dimensions.
- **Bayesian search** (for example **TPE**, Tree-structured Parzen Estimator) uses results of past trials to pick the next promising point. It typically reaches a good configuration in fewer trials than random search, but trials are partly sequential because each uses earlier results.

sections.heading: Hyperopt fmin
sections.body:
```python
from hyperopt import fmin, tpe, hp, SparkTrials, STATUS_OK
import mlflow

space = {
  "max_depth": hp.quniform("max_depth", 2, 12, 1),
  "learning_rate": hp.loguniform("learning_rate", -5, 0),
}

def objective(params):
    auc = train_and_score(params)           # your sklearn / xgboost code
    return {"loss": -auc, "status": STATUS_OK}

with mlflow.start_run():
    best = fmin(fn=objective, space=space, algo=tpe.suggest,
                max_evals=64, trials=SparkTrials(parallelism=8))
```

- `fn` returns a value to **minimise** (a scalar or a dict with `loss`). To maximise AUC or F1, return its **negative**.
- `algo`: `tpe.suggest` for Bayesian TPE, `rand.suggest` for random search.
- `max_evals` is the total number of trials.
- With MLflow, the `fmin` call is logged as a **parent run with one child run per trial**.

sections.heading: SparkTrials vs Trials
sections.body:
- **SparkTrials** distributes trials of **single-machine** models (scikit-learn, single-node XGBoost) across the Spark workers: each trial runs as a task, so many models train at once. Its `parallelism` defaults to the number of executors and has a maximum of 128; a `timeout` can be set.
- For algorithms that are **already distributed** (Spark MLlib, Horovod), do **not** use SparkTrials. Use the default **Trials** class, so trials run one after another on the driver while each training job uses the cluster.
- Higher parallelism finishes faster but gives TPE less feedback between trials, so adaptive search becomes closer to random. Keep parallelism well below `max_evals`.

sections.heading: Hyperopt status on Databricks
sections.body: Databricks docs state that the open-source Hyperopt project is no longer maintained and that Hyperopt is **not included in Databricks Runtime ML after 16.4 LTS ML**. The exam guide still names Hyperopt `fmin`, so know its API, but for new work Databricks recommends **Optuna** or Ray Tune (next lesson).

keyPoints: Grid = exhaustive, random = sampled, Bayesian (TPE) = uses past trial results to choose the next.
fmin minimises the objective; return negative AUC/F1 to maximise them.
tpe.suggest is Bayesian; rand.suggest is random.
SparkTrials parallelises single-node models across workers; use Trials for distributed MLlib training.
Hyperopt is deprecated and not in DBR ML after 16.4 LTS; Optuna is the recommended replacement.

gotchas.trap: Return AUC from the objective so fmin finds the highest AUC.
gotchas.correct: fmin always minimises; return -AUC (or 1 - AUC) as the loss.

gotchas.trap: Use SparkTrials to speed up tuning a Spark MLlib GBTClassifier.
gotchas.correct: MLlib already distributes training; use the default Trials class.

gotchas.trap: Setting parallelism equal to max_evals makes TPE both fastest and smartest.
gotchas.correct: All trials then start without feedback, so TPE behaves like random search.

lessons.lab: Tune a scikit-learn RandomForestClassifier with Hyperopt fmin, tpe.suggest and SparkTrials(parallelism=4) on a DBR ML runtime that still includes Hyperopt (16.4 LTS ML or earlier). Open the MLflow experiment and confirm one parent run with a child run per trial.

lessons.title: Optuna, cross-validation and counting models
lessons.summary: The tuning approach Databricks now recommends (Optuna with MLflow and Spark), plus the Spark ML tuners: CrossValidator vs TrainValidationSplit and how to count the models a search trains.

sections.heading: Optuna on Databricks
sections.body:
- Databricks recommends **Optuna** (or Ray Tune) for single-node tuning now that Hyperopt is unmaintained.
- The objective receives a `trial` and samples values with `trial.suggest_int`, `trial.suggest_float(..., log=True)` and `trial.suggest_categorical`, then returns the metric. A study can be set to minimise or maximise.
- In Optuna itself, the default sampler is **TPESampler** (Bayesian) and the default pruner is **MedianPruner**, which stops unpromising trials early.
- For parallel trials on Spark, Databricks provides `MlflowStorage` (MLflow tracking as the Optuna storage) and `MlflowSparkStudy(...).optimize(objective, n_trials=..., n_jobs=...)`, which runs trials on Spark executors. Optuna can also parallelise with Joblib.

sections.heading: CrossValidator vs TrainValidationSplit
sections.body:
- **CrossValidator** splits data into **k folds**. For each parameter combination it trains k models (each on k−1 folds, evaluated on the held-out fold) and averages the metric. It then **refits the best combination on the entire dataset**.
- **TrainValidationSplit** evaluates each combination **once** on a single split controlled by `trainRatio` (for example 0.75). It is about k times cheaper, but the estimate is noisier, especially on small datasets. It also refits the best combination on all the data.
- Both take `estimator` (a model or a whole Pipeline), `estimatorParamMaps` (from `ParamGridBuilder`), an `evaluator`, and a `parallelism` setting to evaluate parameter sets in parallel; the Spark docs say a value up to 10 is sufficient for most clusters.

| | CrossValidator | TrainValidationSplit |
|---|---|---|
| Fits per combination | k | 1 |
| Cost | Higher | Lower |
| Estimate reliability | Better, uses all data for validation | Depends on one split |
| Good when | Data is small or medium | Data is large or training is expensive |

sections.heading: Counting models trained
sections.body:
- **Grid size** = product of the number of values for each hyperparameter. Example: 4 values × 3 values = 12 combinations.
- **CrossValidator**: grid size × k. With 12 combinations and 3 folds that is **36** models during the search, plus **1** final refit on the full data = 37 if the question counts the refit.
- **TrainValidationSplit**: grid size × 1 = **12**, plus 1 refit = 13.
- Hyperopt or Optuna: the number of trials (`max_evals` / `n_trials`), each possibly multiplied by k if the objective itself cross-validates.

Always read whether a question asks for models trained **during** the search or **including** the final refit.

keyPoints: Databricks recommends Optuna (default TPESampler, MedianPruner) or Ray Tune for new tuning work.
MlflowSparkStudy with MlflowStorage runs Optuna trials in parallel on Spark executors.
CrossValidator: k fits per combination, averaged, then a refit of the best on all data.
TrainValidationSplit: one fit per combination; cheaper but noisier.
Models during a CV grid search = product of grid values × k (add 1 if the final refit is counted).

gotchas.trap: CrossValidator returns the best of the k fold models.
gotchas.correct: It refits the best parameter combination on the full dataset and returns that model.

gotchas.trap: Grid size is the sum of values per hyperparameter.
gotchas.correct: It is the product: 3 values × 4 values = 12 combinations.

gotchas.trap: TrainValidationSplit is the more reliable choice on a small dataset.
gotchas.correct: On small data, k-fold cross-validation gives a more reliable estimate because every row is used for validation once.

lessons.title: Classification and regression metrics, and choosing one
lessons.summary: What F1, log loss, ROC/AUC, PR-AUC, RMSE, MAE and R² measure, how they are configured in Spark evaluators, and how to pick the metric that matches the business cost.

sections.heading: Classification metrics
sections.body:
- **Accuracy**: share of correct predictions. Misleading when classes are imbalanced.
- **Precision**: of predicted positives, how many are real. Matters when false positives are costly.
- **Recall**: of real positives, how many were found. Matters when false negatives are costly.
- **F1**: harmonic mean of precision and recall. A single number that is low if either is low; good for imbalanced data at a chosen threshold.
- **Log loss**: evaluates predicted **probabilities**; heavily penalises confident wrong predictions. Use when calibrated probabilities matter (pricing, risk scores).
- **ROC AUC**: probability that a random positive is ranked above a random negative. **Threshold-independent**. Under heavy imbalance, **PR AUC** (area under precision-recall) is more informative because it focuses on the positive class.

sections.heading: Regression metrics
sections.body:
- **RMSE**: square root of mean squared error, in the target's units. Squaring makes it **penalise large errors** strongly.
- **MAE**: mean absolute error, in target units. Every unit of error counts the same, so it is **more robust to outliers**.
- **R²**: share of the target's variance explained by the model. 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than predicting the mean, and it can be negative on validation data for a very poor model. Unitless, so it is handy for comparing across targets but hides the size of errors.

sections.heading: Spark evaluators
sections.body:
- `BinaryClassificationEvaluator`: default metric `areaUnderROC`; also `areaUnderPR`.
- `MulticlassClassificationEvaluator`: metrics include `f1` (the default), `accuracy`, `weightedPrecision`, `weightedRecall` and `logLoss`.
- `RegressionEvaluator`: default `rmse`; also `mse`, `mae` and `r2`.
- Change the metric with `setMetricName` or the `metricName` parameter. Tuners such as CrossValidator use `evaluator.isLargerBetter()` to know whether to maximise (AUC, F1, R²) or minimise (RMSE, MAE, log loss).

sections.heading: Choosing a metric
sections.body:
Match the metric to the cost of mistakes:

- Missing a positive is expensive (fraud, disease) → **recall**, or F1/PR AUC with recall in mind.
- False alarms are expensive (blocking a good customer) → **precision**.
- Ranking customers for a campaign with a threshold chosen later → **ROC AUC** (or PR AUC if positives are rare).
- Probabilities feed a downstream calculation → **log loss**.
- Large errors are disproportionately bad (under-stocking) → **RMSE**; occasional extreme values should not dominate → **MAE**.
- Explaining "how much variation we capture" to stakeholders → **R²**, alongside an error metric.

keyPoints: F1 balances precision and recall; accuracy misleads under imbalance.
Log loss scores probability quality and punishes confident mistakes.
ROC AUC is threshold-independent; PR AUC is preferred when positives are rare.
RMSE penalises large errors; MAE is robust to outliers; R² is the share of variance explained.
Spark defaults: BinaryClassificationEvaluator = areaUnderROC, MulticlassClassificationEvaluator = f1, RegressionEvaluator = rmse.

gotchas.trap: A higher RMSE than MAE on the same predictions means a bug.
gotchas.correct: RMSE is always ≥ MAE; a large gap simply indicates some large errors.

gotchas.trap: ROC AUC depends on the 0.5 threshold.
gotchas.correct: AUC summarises ranking quality across all thresholds.

gotchas.trap: R² of 0.9 means predictions are within 10% of the truth.
gotchas.correct: R² is variance explained, not a percentage error; check RMSE or MAE for error size.

lessons.lab: Score a binary classifier with BinaryClassificationEvaluator using areaUnderROC and areaUnderPR, then score a regression model with RegressionEvaluator for rmse, mae and r2. Add one extreme outlier to the regression labels and watch which metric moves most.

lessons.title: Log-transformed targets and the bias-variance trade-off
lessons.summary: Why predictions from a model trained on log(target) must be exponentiated before computing RMSE or MAE, and how to diagnose underfitting vs overfitting from training and validation error.

sections.heading: Training on a log-transformed label
sections.body:
A right-skewed, positive target (incomes, sale amounts, claim sizes) is often modelled as `log(y)` (or `log1p(y)` if zeros occur). The model then predicts in **log space**.

Before evaluating or reporting:

1. Convert predictions back with `exp` (or `expm1` if you used `log1p`).
2. Compute RMSE, MAE or R² against the **original-scale** label.

An RMSE computed on log-scale predictions is in "log units". It cannot be compared with a model trained on the raw label, and it understates how wrong the model is in currency terms. In Spark, add a column such as `F.exp("prediction")` and point `RegressionEvaluator` at it and at the original label column.

sections.heading: Bias and variance
sections.body:
- **High bias (underfitting)**: the model is too simple. **Training error is high and validation error is similarly high.** Fixes: a more expressive model, more or better features, less regularisation, deeper trees.
- **High variance (overfitting)**: the model memorises noise. **Training error is low but validation error is much higher.** Fixes: simplify (shallower trees, fewer features), stronger regularisation, more training data, early stopping, ensembling by bagging.
- As model complexity grows, training error keeps falling while validation error falls and then rises. The sweet spot is the complexity with the lowest validation error.

sections.heading: Complexity knobs you can name
sections.body:
- Trees: `maxDepth`, minimum instances per node, number of trees (more bagged trees reduce variance; more boosting rounds can increase it).
- Linear models: `regParam` and `elasticNetParam` in Spark ML (L2 / L1 regularisation).
- Tuning these with cross-validation is how you choose the trade-off empirically rather than by guesswork.

keyPoints: If the model was trained on log(y), exponentiate predictions before computing RMSE/MAE/R².
Use expm1 to invert log1p.
High bias: training and validation errors both high → add complexity or features.
High variance: low training error, much higher validation error → simplify, regularise or add data.
Choose complexity by the lowest validation (or cross-validated) error.

gotchas.trap: Report the RMSE computed directly on the log-scale predictions to business users.
gotchas.correct: Exponentiate predictions first so the error is in the original units.

gotchas.trap: An overfitting model needs more features and deeper trees.
gotchas.correct: Overfitting calls for less complexity, more regularisation or more data.

gotchas.trap: Very low training error proves the model is good.
gotchas.correct: Only validation or test error shows generalisation; a big train-validation gap signals overfitting.

lessons.lab: Train a GBTRegressor on log1p(label), evaluate RMSE once on raw predictions and once after expm1, then sweep maxDepth from 2 to 10 and plot training vs validation RMSE to locate the bias-variance sweet spot.

lessons.title: Batch, streaming and pandas inference
lessons.summary: How to pick batch, streaming or real-time serving, and how to run batch inference with pandas, Spark UDFs, feature tables and ai_query, and streaming inference inside a Lakeflow pipeline (formerly DLT).

sections.heading: Three serving modes and how to choose
sections.body:
The exam asks you to match a requirement to a serving mode. Decide on **latency** first, then on **how the data arrives**:

| Mode | Latency | Typical shape | Databricks tool |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Batch** | Minutes to hours | Score a whole table on a schedule | Job running `spark_udf`, `fe.score_batch` or `ai_query` |
| **Streaming** | Seconds to minutes | Records arrive continuously; results land in a table | Structured Streaming or a Lakeflow pipeline |
| **Real-time** | Milliseconds per request | An application asks for one prediction and waits | Model Serving REST endpoint |

Rules of thumb:

- If nobody waits on the answer and a schedule is acceptable, choose **batch**. It is the cheapest and simplest.
- If events never stop and the result is consumed from a table or dashboard, choose **streaming**.
- If a user or system blocks until the prediction returns (a page load, a payment authorisation), choose **real-time**.
- Fraud can be either: blocking a card payment before approval is real-time; flagging suspicious events for analysts a minute later is streaming.

sections.heading: Batch inference with pandas
sections.body:
Every MLflow model can be loaded through the generic **pyfunc** flavour, and the MLflow docs state that all PyFunc models support a `pandas.DataFrame` as input. This is the simplest batch pattern for data that fits in memory on one machine:

```python
import mlflow
model = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("models:/main.ml.claims_risk@Champion")
preds = model.predict(pdf)   # pdf is a pandas DataFrame
```

Notes:

- Models in Unity Catalog are addressed as `models:/<catalog>.<schema>.<model>@<alias>` or `.../<version>`. Stage URIs such as `models:/name/Production` do not work, because UC does not support stages.
- This runs on the **driver only**. Calling `toPandas()` on a very large Spark DataFrame to use this pattern can exhaust driver memory.

sections.heading: Batch inference at Spark scale
sections.body:
For tables too large for one machine, wrap the model as a Spark UDF so that executors score partitions in parallel:

```python
predict = mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf(spark, "models:/main.ml.claims_risk@Champion", result_type="double")
scored = df.withColumn("risk", predict(*feature_cols))
scored.write.mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("main.ml.claims_scored")
```

Other batch options you should recognise:

- **`fe.score_batch(model_uri=..., df=...)`** for a model logged with `FeatureEngineeringClient.log_model`. You pass only the lookup keys (plus any request-time columns); the client looks up the remaining features from the feature tables. Values supplied in `df` override the lookup.
- **`ai_query`** in SQL calls a serving endpoint for every row of a query. Databricks' model inference docs now recommend AI Functions for batch inference against serving endpoints.

sections.heading: Streaming inference in a Lakeflow pipeline
sections.body:
Delta Live Tables (DLT) is now called **Lakeflow pipelines**, built on Spark Declarative Pipelines. The exam guide still says "DLT"; treat the names as the same thing. To score a stream, load the model as a Spark UDF and apply it inside a **streaming table** definition:

```python
from pyspark import pipelines as dp
import mlflow

score = mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf(spark, "models:/main.ml.sensor_anomaly@Champion")

@dp.table(comment="Sensor readings with anomaly scores")
def scored_readings():
    return (spark.readStream.table("main.iot.readings")
            .withColumn("anomaly", score("temp", "vibration", "rpm")))
```

Why a pipeline rather than a hand-written job: the pipeline manages checkpoints, dependencies and **enhanced autoscaling** for you.

Syntax to know:

- `@dp.table` defines a streaming table, `@dp.materialized_view` a materialized view, and `@dp.temporary_view` a view that is not published.
- Existing code that uses `import dlt` and `@dlt.table` keeps working. No migration is required.

keyPoints: Latency decides the mode: batch for scheduled tables, streaming for continuous arrival read from tables, real-time for request/response.
mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(uri).predict(pandas_df) is single-machine batch inference.
mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf distributes scoring across executors for large tables and for streams.
fe.score_batch looks up feature-table features automatically for models logged with fe.log_model.
Streaming inference in a Lakeflow pipeline is a spark_udf applied in an @dp.table over a streaming source.
UC model URIs use aliases or versions, never stage names.

gotchas.trap: Calling a real-time endpoint row by row from a loop to score a large weekly table.
gotchas.correct: Use batch scoring with spark_udf (or ai_query in SQL) on a scheduled job.

gotchas.trap: Calling toPandas() on a billion-row table so you can call predict().
gotchas.correct: Wrap the model with mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf and score on the executors.

gotchas.trap: Loading models:/catalog.schema.model/Production.
gotchas.correct: Unity Catalog uses aliases: models:/catalog.schema.model@Champion.

gotchas.trap: Assuming code written with import dlt must be rewritten after the rename.
gotchas.correct: Legacy dlt code still works; from pyspark import pipelines as dp is the current style.

lessons.lab: Register any small scikit-learn model in Unity Catalog with an alias. Score a pandas DataFrame with mlflow.pyfunc.load_model, then score a Spark table with mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf and write the result to a Delta table. Finally, create a Lakeflow pipeline with one @dp.table that reads a table as a stream and adds a prediction column with the same UDF.

lessons.title: Model Serving: deploy, query and split traffic
lessons.summary: Deploying a custom MLflow model from Unity Catalog to a Model Serving endpoint, querying it over REST, SQL and the MLflow deployments client, and splitting traffic between a champion and a challenger.

sections.heading: What Model Serving does
sections.body:
Model Serving exposes each served model as a **REST API** on serverless, autoscaling compute. It serves three kinds of model:

- **Custom models**: MLflow-format Python models registered in Unity Catalog (or the legacy workspace registry). Agents are also served as custom models.
- **Foundation Model APIs**: pay-per-token or provisioned throughput.
- **External models**: models hosted by other providers, governed centrally.

The exam focuses on custom models. One endpoint cannot mix model types, so a custom model and an external model cannot share an endpoint.

sections.heading: Packaging and deploying a custom model
sections.body:
A custom model is often a `mlflow.pyfunc.PythonModel` subclass. Use it when you need preprocessing or postprocessing around the estimator:

```python
class RiskModel(mlflow.pyfunc.PythonModel):
    def load_context(self, context):
        ...  # load artifacts once
    def predict(self, context, model_input):
        ...  # return predictions for a pandas DataFrame

mlflow.pyfunc.log_model(name="risk", python_model=RiskModel(),
                        input_example=sample_pdf,
                        registered_model_name="main.ml.claims_risk")
```

The deployment steps are:

1. Log the model with a **signature**. New model versions in Unity Catalog must have one, and an `input_example` lets MLflow infer it.
2. Register it in UC as `catalog.schema.model`.
3. Create an endpoint (UI, or `POST /api/2.0/serving-endpoints`) whose **served entity** names the UC model and a specific version.

```json
{"name": "claims-risk",
 "config": {"served_entities": [
   {"name": "champion", "entity_name": "main.ml.claims_risk",
    "entity_version": "3", "workload_size": "Small",
    "scale_to_zero_enabled": true}]}}
```

sections.heading: Querying an endpoint
sections.body:
Send `POST https://<workspace-url>/serving-endpoints/<endpoint-name>/invocations` with a bearer token. Databricks recommends **OAuth machine-to-machine** (a service principal) for production, and route-optimised endpoints accept only OAuth.

Input formats for custom models:

- `dataframe_split`: columns plus data. **Recommended**, and preserves column order.
- `dataframe_records`: a list of row objects. Column order is not guaranteed.
- `instances`: tensor input, row-based.
- `inputs`: tensor input, columnar.

```json
{"dataframe_split": {"columns": ["age", "claims_3y"], "data": [[42, 1], [29, 0]]}}
```

The response wraps the output in a `predictions` key. Other ways to query:

- `mlflow.deployments.get_deploy_client("databricks").predict(endpoint="claims-risk", inputs={...})` from Python.
- `ai_query('claims-risk', ...)` from SQL.
- **Query endpoint** in the Serving UI.

sections.heading: Splitting traffic between models
sections.body:
One endpoint can serve several entities, for example the current champion version and a challenger version. The `traffic_config` decides how requests are shared:

```json
"traffic_config": {"routes": [
  {"served_model_name": "champion",   "traffic_percentage": 90},
  {"served_model_name": "challenger", "traffic_percentage": 10}]}
```

- Clients keep calling the same `/invocations` URL; the endpoint routes each request by the percentages.
- Change the split with `PUT /api/2.0/serving-endpoints/{name}/config` or with **Edit configuration** in the UI. Shift traffic gradually (90/10, 50/50, 0/100) as the challenger proves itself.
- To test one model on its own, call `/serving-endpoints/{endpoint}/served-models/{served-model}/invocations`. This **bypasses** the traffic split.
- Registry stages play no part. In Unity Catalog, aliases such as `Champion` label versions, but the endpoint serves the versions named in its configuration.

sections.heading: Features at serving time
sections.body: If the model was trained with feature tables and logged with `fe.log_model`, the endpoint can look features up for each request. Publish the feature table to a **Databricks Online Feature Store** (a low-latency copy powered by Lakebase) with `fe.publish_table`. Model Serving then looks up the published features automatically, and the client sends only the lookup keys. The offline Delta feature table remains the source of truth for training and batch scoring. Legacy "online tables" are retired.

keyPoints: Custom models = MLflow Python models from Unity Catalog, served as REST endpoints on serverless autoscaling compute.
UC model versions need a signature; an input_example lets MLflow infer it.
Query with POST /serving-endpoints/<name>/invocations; dataframe_split is the recommended format; output is under predictions.
Use OAuth M2M with a service principal for production callers.
traffic_config.routes sets served_model_name and traffic_percentage for A/B or canary rollouts; update with PUT .../config.
The served-models/<name>/invocations URL hits one model and bypasses the split.
Publish feature tables to an Online Feature Store so the endpoint can look up features from keys.

gotchas.trap: Creating a second endpoint and asking clients to pick one at random to run an A/B test.
gotchas.correct: Serve both versions on one endpoint and set traffic_config routes.

gotchas.trap: Using dataframe_records when column order matters.
gotchas.correct: Use dataframe_split, which Databricks recommends.

gotchas.trap: Embedding a data scientist's personal access token in a production service.
gotchas.correct: Use OAuth M2M with a service principal.

gotchas.trap: Transitioning a version to the Production stage to deploy it.
gotchas.correct: UC has no stages; the endpoint config names the model version to serve.

lessons.lab: Wrap a scikit-learn model in a PythonModel that scales inputs before predicting, log it with an input_example, and register it in Unity Catalog. Create an endpoint serving version 1, query it with curl using dataframe_split, then register version 2, add it as a second served entity, and route 80/20 between them. Query the served-models URL of version 2 directly and compare.
