flashcards.front: What does Databricks Runtime for ML add over the standard runtime?
flashcards.back: Preinstalled, compatible ML and deep learning libraries plus MLflow integration, so you can train without installing and pinning packages.

flashcards.front: Which access mode does the Machine learning checkbox select?
flashcards.back: Dedicated (formerly single user).

flashcards.front: Which access mode does not support AutoML?
flashcards.back: Standard (formerly shared).

flashcards.front: Does Photon speed up single-node PyTorch or scikit-learn training?
flashcards.back: No. Photon accelerates Spark SQL, DataFrames and feature engineering, not single-node Python libraries.

flashcards.front: When are top-tier libraries added or removed from DBR ML?
flashcards.back: Only with major runtime releases.

flashcards.front: Three problem types supported by AutoML?
flashcards.back: Classification, regression and forecasting.

flashcards.front: Why is AutoML called a "glass box"?
flashcards.back: It generates an editable source notebook for every trial, so you see and can modify the code behind each model.

flashcards.front: Which AutoML notebooks are imported automatically for classification/regression?
flashcards.back: The data exploration notebook and the best trial notebook. Other trials are stored as MLflow artifacts.

flashcards.front: How is each AutoML trial recorded?
flashcards.back: As an MLflow run, with metrics, parameters and the model.

flashcards.front: How do you enable SHAP in an AutoML trial notebook?
flashcards.back: Set shap_enabled = True; the code is included but off by default.

flashcards.front: Name two forecasting algorithms AutoML uses.
flashcards.back: Prophet and Auto-ARIMA (serverless forecasting adds DeepAR).

flashcards.front: Which MLOps deployment pattern does Databricks recommend in most cases?
flashcards.back: Deploy code: promote training code and retrain in each environment.

flashcards.front: Name two situations where deploying models is preferred.
flashcards.back: Very expensive or hard-to-reproduce training; single workspace; no external repos or CI/CD.

flashcards.front: Main data advantage of the deploy-code pattern?
flashcards.back: Production data can stay in the production environment; the model is retrained there.

flashcards.front: What usually represents an environment (dev/staging/prod) in Unity Catalog?
flashcards.back: A catalog.

flashcards.front: What is the hybrid deployment pattern?
flashcards.back: Deploy code to staging, train there, then deploy the resulting model to prod.

flashcards.front: What makes a UC Delta table a feature table?
flashcards.back: A primary key constraint.

flashcards.front: Import and construct the UC feature engineering client.
flashcards.back: from databricks.feature_engineering import FeatureEngineeringClient; fe = FeatureEngineeringClient()

flashcards.front: How do you pass a composite primary key to fe.create_table?
flashcards.back: As a list, e.g. primary_keys=["store_id", "sku"].

flashcards.front: What must be true of a column before it becomes a primary key?
flashcards.back: It must be NOT NULL (ALTER COLUMN ... SET NOT NULL).

flashcards.front: What does fe.write_table(mode="merge") do to rows whose keys are absent from the DataFrame?
flashcards.back: Leaves them unchanged; merge upserts by key.

flashcards.front: What does timeseries_columns / a TIMESERIES key enable?
flashcards.back: Point-in-time lookups so training does not use feature values from the future.

flashcards.front: Which object describes which features to join from a feature table?
flashcards.back: FeatureLookup(table_name, feature_names, lookup_key, timestamp_lookup_key, ...).

flashcards.front: Which call builds a training set from labels plus feature lookups?
flashcards.back: fe.create_training_set(df=labels_df, feature_lookups=[...], label="y"), then .load_df().

flashcards.front: Why log with fe.log_model instead of mlflow.<flavor>.log_model?
flashcards.back: fe.log_model packages feature lookup metadata so scoring can fetch features automatically.

flashcards.front: What does fe.score_batch need in the input DataFrame?
flashcards.back: Only the lookup keys; features are looked up. Supplied feature columns override the lookup.

flashcards.front: Status of the Workspace Feature Store?
flashcards.back: Deprecated; only for workspaces without Unity Catalog.

flashcards.front: Key benefit of account-level (UC) feature tables over workspace ones?
flashcards.back: Sharing across workspaces on the same metastore, plus centralised governance and lineage.

flashcards.front: Offline vs online feature table purpose?
flashcards.back: Offline (Delta) = source of truth for training and batch scoring. Online = low-latency copy for real-time serving.

flashcards.front: What powers Databricks Online Feature Stores?
flashcards.back: Lakebase.

flashcards.front: Three publish modes for fe.publish_table?
flashcards.back: TRIGGERED (default), CONTINUOUS and SNAPSHOT.

flashcards.front: What must be enabled on a source table for TRIGGERED or CONTINUOUS publishing?
flashcards.back: Change Data Feed.

flashcards.front: Difference between params and metrics in MLflow?
flashcards.back: Params are inputs such as hyperparameters; metrics are numeric results, optionally per step.

flashcards.front: Which call logs a local file such as a PNG to the current run?
flashcards.back: mlflow.log_artifact(local_path).

flashcards.front: MLflow 3 replacement for log_model(artifact_path=...)?
flashcards.back: log_model(..., name=...).

flashcards.front: How do you find the run with the lowest validation RMSE via the client?
flashcards.back: MlflowClient().search_runs(experiment_ids=[...], order_by=["metrics.val_rmse ASC"], max_results=1).

flashcards.front: What does mlflow.search_runs return?
flashcards.back: A pandas DataFrame of runs.

flashcards.front: Name four things the MLflow UI shows for a run.
flashcards.back: Parameters, metrics with charts, tags, artifacts (model, signature), source notebook, start time, duration, user.

flashcards.front: What must every new model version in UC have?
flashcards.back: A model signature (from autologging or an input_example).

flashcards.front: URI that loads the champion version of a UC model?
flashcards.back: models:/<catalog>.<schema>.<model>@Champion

flashcards.front: How do you promote a challenger to champion in UC?
flashcards.back: client.set_registered_model_alias(name, "Champion", challenger_version) — the alias moves to that version.

flashcards.front: Method to remove a tag from one model version?
flashcards.back: client.delete_model_version_tag(name, version, key).

flashcards.front: Which statistics does Spark DataFrame.summary() return by default?
flashcards.back: count, mean, stddev, min, 25%, 50%, 75% and max. The percentiles are approximate.

flashcards.front: How does describe() differ from summary() in PySpark?
flashcards.back: describe() returns only count, mean, stddev, min and max; summary() adds the 25%, 50% and 75% percentiles and lets you request custom statistics.

flashcards.front: How do you ask summary() for custom percentiles?
flashcards.back: Pass them as strings, for example df.summary("count", "10%", "90%").

flashcards.front: What does dbutils.data.summarize(df) do?
flashcards.back: Computes and displays summary statistics and histograms for a Spark or pandas DataFrame in a Databricks notebook, scanning the whole DataFrame.

flashcards.front: What does precise=True change in dbutils.data.summarize?
flashcards.back: Statistics such as distinct counts become exact; histograms and percentiles remain approximate but with much smaller error.

flashcards.front: Standard-deviation outlier rule
flashcards.back: Keep values within mean ± k·stddev, commonly k = 3. Assumes a roughly symmetric distribution.

flashcards.front: IQR outlier rule
flashcards.back: IQR = Q3 − Q1; keep values within [Q1 − 1.5·IQR, Q3 + 1.5·IQR]. Robust to skew and extremes.

flashcards.front: How do you get quartiles of a Spark column for the IQR rule?
flashcards.back: df.approxQuantile("col", [0.25, 0.75], relativeError); relativeError = 0 is exact but expensive. In SQL: percentile_approx.

flashcards.front: Why is the IQR rule preferred over the 3σ rule for skewed data?
flashcards.back: Quartiles are barely affected by extreme values, while the mean and stddev are inflated by them, which distorts 3σ bounds.

flashcards.front: Best plot for one continuous feature
flashcards.back: Histogram, density plot or box plot.

flashcards.front: Best way to compare two categorical features
flashcards.back: A contingency table (crosstab) or stacked bar chart, with a chi-square test of independence.

flashcards.front: Pearson vs Spearman correlation
flashcards.back: Pearson measures linear association on raw values; Spearman measures monotonic association on ranks and is more robust to outliers.

flashcards.front: Best plot for a continuous feature against a categorical one
flashcards.back: Grouped (side-by-side) box plots, one per category.

flashcards.front: When should you impute with the median instead of the mean?
flashcards.back: When the continuous feature is skewed or has outliers, since the median is robust to extreme values.

flashcards.front: When should you impute with the mode?
flashcards.back: For categorical or discrete features, using the most frequent value.

flashcards.front: Spark ML Imputer strategies and default
flashcards.back: strategy = "mean" (default), "median" or "mode". Inputs must be numeric columns.

flashcards.front: Why must Imputer be fitted on training data only?
flashcards.back: It is an Estimator whose fit() learns the fill value; fitting on all data leaks test-set information into training.

flashcards.front: Order of stages to one-hot encode a string column in Spark ML
flashcards.back: StringIndexer → OneHotEncoder → VectorAssembler.

flashcards.front: What does OneHotEncoder dropLast=True do?
flashcards.back: Drops the last category column (default) so the encoded columns are not perfectly collinear; the dropped category is all zeros.

flashcards.front: When is one-hot encoding a poor choice?
flashcards.back: For high-cardinality features, usually for tree-based models, and for ordinal features where order matters.

flashcards.front: When is a log transform appropriate, and how do you handle zeros?
flashcards.back: For right-skewed, positive data spanning orders of magnitude (prices, incomes, counts). Use log1p when zeros are present; negatives are undefined.

flashcards.front: A model was trained on log1p(target). What must you do before computing RMSE in original units?
flashcards.back: Apply expm1 (the inverse of log1p) to the predictions first.

flashcards.front: What does a Spark ML Transformer implement?
flashcards.back: transform(): it takes a DataFrame and returns a new DataFrame, usually with extra columns. Fitted models are Transformers.

flashcards.front: What does a Spark ML Estimator implement?
flashcards.back: fit(): it learns from a DataFrame and returns a Model, which is a Transformer.

flashcards.front: Is a Spark ML Pipeline an Estimator or a Transformer?
flashcards.back: An Estimator. Pipeline.fit() returns a PipelineModel, which is a Transformer.

flashcards.front: Is StringIndexer an Estimator or a Transformer?
flashcards.back: An Estimator: it learns the category-to-index mapping and returns a StringIndexerModel.

flashcards.front: Is VectorAssembler an Estimator or a Transformer?
flashcards.back: A Transformer: it combines columns into a vector without learning anything from data.

flashcards.front: Why put preprocessing inside a Pipeline before tuning?
flashcards.back: Preprocessing is then fit on training folds only and refit per fold, avoiding leakage, and the same steps run at inference.

flashcards.front: Why is accuracy a poor metric for a 1%-positive problem?
flashcards.back: Predicting the majority class always scores 99% accuracy while catching no positives.

flashcards.front: Name two training-time fixes for class imbalance.
flashcards.back: Class weights / cost-sensitive learning (e.g. weightCol, class_weight) and resampling the training data (oversample, undersample, SMOTE).

flashcards.front: When should resampling for imbalance happen relative to the train/validation split?
flashcards.back: After the split, on the training data only.

flashcards.front: What does grid search do?
flashcards.back: Tries every combination of a discrete set of hyperparameter values.

flashcards.front: Why is random search often better than grid search for the same budget?
flashcards.back: It samples more distinct values of each important hyperparameter instead of repeating values across a grid.

flashcards.front: What makes Bayesian search (e.g. TPE) different from random search?
flashcards.back: It uses results of previous trials to choose the next promising configuration.

flashcards.front: Does Hyperopt fmin minimise or maximise?
flashcards.back: Minimise. Return the negative of a metric you want to maximise, such as -AUC.

flashcards.front: Which Hyperopt algo setting gives Bayesian TPE search?
flashcards.back: algo=tpe.suggest (rand.suggest gives random search).

flashcards.front: What does Hyperopt SparkTrials do?
flashcards.back: Runs trials of single-machine models in parallel as tasks on Spark workers.

flashcards.front: Which Trials class should you use with Spark MLlib in Hyperopt?
flashcards.back: The default Trials class, because MLlib training is already distributed.

flashcards.front: How is a Hyperopt fmin run with MLflow organised?
flashcards.back: As a parent run with one child run per trial.

flashcards.front: What is the status of Hyperopt in Databricks Runtime ML?
flashcards.back: Deprecated and unmaintained upstream; not included in DBR ML after 16.4 LTS ML. Databricks recommends Optuna or Ray Tune.

flashcards.front: What are Optuna’s default sampler and pruner?
flashcards.back: TPESampler (Bayesian) and MedianPruner.

flashcards.front: How do you run Optuna trials in parallel on Spark in Databricks?
flashcards.back: Use MlflowStorage as the study storage and MlflowSparkStudy(...).optimize(objective, n_trials=..., n_jobs=...).

flashcards.front: What does CrossValidator return after the search?
flashcards.back: A model refit on the full dataset with the best parameter combination.

flashcards.front: How many fits does TrainValidationSplit do per parameter combination?
flashcards.back: One, on a single train/validation split set by trainRatio.

flashcards.front: Main trade-off: CrossValidator vs TrainValidationSplit?
flashcards.back: CV is more reliable (every row validates once) but about k times more expensive; TVS is cheaper but noisier.

flashcards.front: Models trained in a CV grid search with 5 × 2 values and 4 folds (excluding the refit)?
flashcards.back: 5 × 2 = 10 combinations × 4 folds = 40 models (41 with the final refit).

flashcards.front: What does the parallelism parameter on CrossValidator control?
flashcards.back: How many parameter combinations are evaluated in parallel; Spark docs say up to 10 is sufficient for most clusters.

flashcards.front: What is F1?
flashcards.back: The harmonic mean of precision and recall.

flashcards.front: What does log loss evaluate?
flashcards.back: The quality of predicted probabilities; it heavily penalises confident wrong predictions.

flashcards.front: Why prefer PR AUC over ROC AUC under heavy imbalance?
flashcards.back: PR AUC focuses on the positive class, so it is not flattered by the many easy true negatives.

flashcards.front: RMSE vs MAE: which is more sensitive to large errors?
flashcards.back: RMSE, because errors are squared before averaging.

flashcards.front: What does R² measure?
flashcards.back: The proportion of variance in the target explained by the model (1 = perfect, 0 = no better than the mean).

flashcards.front: Default metric of BinaryClassificationEvaluator?
flashcards.back: areaUnderROC.

flashcards.front: Default metric of RegressionEvaluator?
flashcards.back: rmse.

flashcards.front: Default metric of MulticlassClassificationEvaluator?
A model was trained on log(price). What must you do before computing RMSE in price units?
flashcards.back: Exponentiate the predictions (exp, or expm1 if log1p was used) and compare with the original label.

flashcards.front: Low training error, much higher validation error: bias or variance problem?
flashcards.back: High variance (overfitting). Simplify, regularise or add data.

flashcards.front: High training error and similar validation error: bias or variance problem?
flashcards.back: High bias (underfitting). Add complexity or better features.

flashcards.front: Name two Spark ML regularisation parameters for linear models.
flashcards.back: regParam (strength) and elasticNetParam (mix between L2 at 0 and L1 at 1).

flashcards.front: What are the three serving modes, and what decides between them?
flashcards.back: Batch (scheduled table scoring, cheapest), streaming (continuous arrival, seconds to minutes, results in a table) and real-time (millisecond request/response via a REST endpoint). Latency and how data arrives decide.

flashcards.front: How do you run batch inference on a pandas DataFrame with an MLflow model?
flashcards.back: mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("models:/cat.schema.model@alias").predict(pdf). All PyFunc models accept a pandas DataFrame. It runs on one machine.

flashcards.front: What does mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf do?
flashcards.back: Wraps an MLflow model as a Spark UDF so executors score partitions in parallel, for large batch tables or streaming DataFrames: df.withColumn("pred", udf(*cols)).

flashcards.front: How do you batch-score a model that was logged with fe.log_model?
flashcards.back: fe.score_batch(model_uri=..., df=...). Pass the lookup keys; features are looked up from feature tables automatically, and columns you pass override the lookup.

flashcards.front: Which SQL function do Databricks docs recommend for batch inference against a serving endpoint?
flashcards.back: ai_query (AI Functions). It calls the endpoint for each row of a SQL query.

flashcards.front: How do you run streaming inference in a Lakeflow pipeline (formerly DLT)?
flashcards.back: Load the model with mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf and apply it with withColumn inside an @dp.table function that reads a streaming source (spark.readStream).

flashcards.front: Current Python import and decorators for Lakeflow pipelines?
flashcards.back: from pyspark import pipelines as dp; @dp.table (streaming table), @dp.materialized_view, @dp.temporary_view. Legacy import dlt still works without migration.

flashcards.front: What URL does a client call to get predictions from a serving endpoint?
flashcards.back: POST https://<workspace>/serving-endpoints/<endpoint-name>/invocations, authenticated with a Databricks token (OAuth M2M recommended for production).

flashcards.front: Which input formats do custom model endpoints accept, and which is recommended?
flashcards.back: dataframe_split (recommended, keeps column order), dataframe_records (column order not guaranteed), instances (row tensors), inputs (columnar tensors).

flashcards.front: Under which key does a custom model endpoint return its output?
flashcards.back: predictions

flashcards.front: How do you split traffic between two models on one endpoint?
flashcards.back: Serve both as served entities and set config.traffic_config.routes, e.g. [{served_model_name: "champion", traffic_percentage: 90}, {served_model_name: "challenger", traffic_percentage: 10}].

flashcards.front: How do you change an existing traffic split?
flashcards.back: PUT /api/2.0/serving-endpoints/{name}/config with the new served entities and routes, or Edit configuration in the Serving UI.

flashcards.front: How do you send a request to one served model and bypass the traffic split?
flashcards.back: Call /serving-endpoints/{endpoint}/served-models/{served-model}/invocations.

flashcards.front: What must a custom pyfunc model have before it is registered in Unity Catalog and served?
flashcards.back: A model signature (inferred from an input_example or autologging). A PythonModel subclass implements predict, and optionally load_context.

flashcards.front: How does a serving endpoint get feature-table features at request time?
flashcards.back: Publish the feature table to a Databricks Online Feature Store with fe.publish_table; Model Serving looks up the published features automatically from the keys in the request.

flashcards.front: Which authentication should a production service use to call Model Serving?
flashcards.back: OAuth machine-to-machine with a service principal. Route-optimised endpoints accept only OAuth.

Create compute with Databricks Runtime for ML selected, so common ML libraries come preinstalled and tested together.

Enable Photon on the standard runtime.

Installing "latest" on startup reintroduces drift and maintenance; it is the anti-pattern DBR ML avoids.
Photon is a query engine accelerator; it does not install ML libraries.

questions.scenario: A product team with limited ML experience wants a strong baseline for a binary classification problem on a UC table, and wants to see and edit the code that produced it.
questions.stem: Which Databricks capability best fits?
options: A Lakeflow pipeline with an expectation on the label column
The Workspace Feature Store, which selects the best features and model automatically
AutoML, which tunes several algorithms and generates an editable notebook for each trial
A Model Serving endpoint with a Foundation Model API

The Workspace Feature Store stores features; it does not train models, and it is deprecated.

questions.scenario: After an AutoML regression experiment finishes on classic compute, a data scientist looks in the workspace for the generated notebooks.
questions.stem: Which notebooks are imported into the workspace automatically?

The data exploration notebook and the best trial notebook; other trials are stored as MLflow artifacts
Every trial notebook, imported into a folder per algorithm
Only the best trial notebook; there is no data exploration notebook

rationales: Notebooks come from the experiment, not from serving.

AutoML also produces a data exploration notebook.

questions.scenario: An analyst starts an AutoML experiment from a compute resource that several colleagues share. The experiment fails to start, although the same dataset works for a teammate on a different cluster.
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause?
options: The shared compute uses Standard access mode, which does not support AutoML.
The dataset has more than one categorical column, which AutoML cannot handle.
AutoML only runs on serverless SQL warehouses.
The analyst has not registered a model in Unity Catalog first.
questions.explanation: AutoML is supported on Dedicated access mode, while Standard (formerly shared) access mode does not support it. A teammate on Dedicated compute would succeed with the same data.
rationales: Correct. AutoML needs Dedicated access mode.
AutoML handles categorical columns as part of data preparation.
AutoML runs on ML compute, not on SQL warehouses.
Registration happens after training; it is not a prerequisite.

questions.stem: Which statements describe what AutoML adds to model development on Databricks? (Select two.)
options: It generates a data exploration notebook that helps identify problematic or useful features.
It removes the need to validate the model, because the best trial is guaranteed to generalise.
It deploys the best model to a serving endpoint automatically when the run completes.
Each trial is tracked as an MLflow run, so results can be compared in the experiment UI.
questions.explanation: AutoML logs every trial to MLflow and produces a data exploration notebook plus trial notebooks, giving a fast, inspectable baseline. Validation and deployment remain the practitioner's responsibility.
rationales: Correct. The exploration notebook supports feature selection.
No tool guarantees generalisation; validation is still required.
AutoML trains and logs models; deployment is a separate step.
Correct. Every AutoML trial is an MLflow run.

questions.scenario: A data scientist installs an extra plotting package and upgrades scikit-learn on the cluster where AutoML experiments run, after which AutoML runs begin to fail.
questions.stem: What is the best course of action?
options: Switch the cluster to Standard access mode to isolate the libraries.
Rewrite the experiment with the Workspace Feature Store client.
Run AutoML on compute without extra or changed libraries, because modifying library versions causes AutoML run failures.
Pin scikit-learn to the newest release on all clusters so AutoML can use new estimators.
questions.explanation: AutoML depends on a specific library set (on the newest runtimes via the databricks-automl-runtime package), and installing extra libraries or changing versions causes failures. Keep AutoML compute clean and do custom work elsewhere.
rationales: Standard access mode does not support AutoML.
The feature store client is unrelated to AutoML library compatibility.
Correct. The docs warn against installing extra libraries or changing versions.
Changing library versions is exactly what breaks AutoML.

questions.scenario: An organisation has separate dev, staging and prod workspaces, a Git repository and a CI/CD system. Production data cannot be read from dev. Training takes about 30 minutes.
questions.stem: Which deployment pattern fits best?
options: Export the model as a pickle file and email it to the prod team.
Deploy code: promote reviewed training code and retrain the model in each environment.
Deploy models: train once in dev and copy the artifact to prod.
Train in prod directly from notebooks without a staging step.
questions.explanation: Databricks recommends deploying code in most situations: training code is reviewed and the model is retrained in each environment, so production data can stay in prod. Cheap training and existing CI/CD remove the usual reasons to deploy models instead.
rationales: Manual hand-offs bypass governance and reproducibility.
Correct. This is the recommended default and keeps prod data in prod.
Not viable when dev cannot access prod data, and unnecessary when training is cheap.
Skipping review and testing is an MLOps anti-pattern.

Deploy code: retrain the model separately in staging and prod on full data.
Avoid the registry and load the model from the training notebook's local disk in prod.
Use AutoML in prod to regenerate the model on each deployment.

Retraining is expensive and not reproducible here, which undermines deploy code.
This bypasses versioning and governance.
Regenerating the model contradicts the constraint that training cannot be reproduced.

It makes automated retraining in production easier than deploy code.
It is the pattern Databricks recommends for most teams.
Supporting code such as inference and monitoring pipelines must still be deployed to production separately.
questions.explanation: With deploy models the artifact is trained in dev, so dev needs the data and other pipelines must be deployed separately. Automated retraining is harder, which is one reason deploy code is the default recommendation.

Automated retraining is tricky with deploy models.
Deploy code is the general recommendation.

Hybrid: deploy code to staging, train there, then deploy the model to prod
Deploy code, because code moved from dev to staging
Deploy models, because a model reached prod

Download the model files and re-upload them with a new name in the prod workspace.

questions.scenario: A data engineer has an existing Delta table `ml.features.store_daily` in Unity Catalog with a non-nullable `store_id` column and wants it to be usable as a feature table.

options: Run ALTER TABLE ml.features.store_daily SET AS FEATURE STORE.
Copy the table into the Workspace Feature Store.
Recreate the table with CREATE TABLE ... USING FEATURE.
Add a primary key constraint on store_id with ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... PRIMARY KEY.
questions.explanation: Any Delta table in Unity Catalog with a primary key constraint is a feature table. Primary key columns must be NOT NULL, which is already satisfied here, so adding the constraint is enough.
rationales: There is no such SQL clause.
The workspace feature store is deprecated and not needed for UC.
There is no FEATURE table format; feature tables are Delta tables.

Convert the table to Parquet before adding the key.
Run ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN session_id SET NOT NULL, then add the primary key constraint.
Add the constraint with the TIMESERIES keyword instead.

questions.scenario: A churn model is trained on labelled events with an event_ts column. Customer features are recomputed daily into a time-series feature table. Validation accuracy is far higher than production accuracy.
questions.stem: Which change most directly addresses the likely cause?
options: Drop the time-series key so the latest feature values are always joined.
Increase the number of trees in the model.
Publish the feature table to an online store before training.
Use a timestamp_lookup_key in the FeatureLookup so training joins feature values as of each event time.
questions.explanation: A large gap between offline and production performance with time-varying features suggests leakage. A time-series feature table plus timestamp_lookup_key performs point-in-time joins so each label sees only feature values available at its event time.
rationales: Joining the latest values is what causes leakage.
Model capacity does not fix leaked features.
Online stores serve real-time lookups; training reads the offline table.

questions.scenario: Quick quartile check
questions.stem: A data scientist wants a fast look at the minimum, maximum and interquartile range of every numeric column in a Spark DataFrame, returned as a DataFrame they can save. Which call fits best?
options: df.describe()
df.groupBy().count()
df.summary()
df.approxQuantile("*", [0.5], 0.0)
questions.explanation: summary() returns count, mean, stddev, min, 25%, 50%, 75% and max by default, so the quartiles needed for the IQR are included. describe() omits the percentiles.
rationales: describe() returns count, mean, stddev, min and max only, with no quartiles.
A global count gives the row count only.
Correct: summary() includes the 25% and 75% percentiles alongside min and max.
approxQuantile takes column names, not a wildcard, and here requests only the median.

questions.scenario: Exact distinct counts
questions.stem: An analyst runs dbutils.data.summarize on a customer table and sees a distinct count of about 1.02 million for customer_id, but expects exactly 1,000,000. What explains this, and how can they get an exact distinct count?
options: summarize samples 10% of rows; increase the sample size
The table has duplicates; run dropDuplicates and summarize again
summarize only works on pandas DataFrames; convert with toPandas()
summarize is approximate by default; rerun with precise=True
questions.explanation: dbutils.data.summarize defaults to precise=False, where distinct counts on high-cardinality columns can be off by around 5%. Setting precise=True makes such counts exact, although histograms and percentiles stay approximate.
rationales: The function scans the whole DataFrame rather than a sample.
Duplicate rows cannot raise a distinct count above the true number of unique IDs; the 2% gap is within the documented approximation error of the default mode.
It accepts both Spark and pandas DataFrames.
Correct: precise=True gives exact distinct counts.

questions.scenario: Percentiles with precise mode
questions.stem: A team runs dbutils.data.summarize(df, precise=True) and reports the 99th percentile of transaction amount as an exact value in a compliance document. What is the problem?
options: precise=True drops null values, which biases percentiles
precise=True is only valid on pandas DataFrames
Percentiles and histograms remain approximate even with precise=True
There is no problem; precise=True makes all statistics exact
questions.explanation: With precise=True, most statistics become exact, but histograms and percentiles are still approximate with a very small error. If an exact percentile is required, compute it with an exact method such as approxQuantile with relativeError = 0.
rationales: Null handling is not what makes the reported value inexact.
The function accepts Spark and pandas DataFrames in either mode.
Correct: percentile estimates stay approximate, only with much lower error.
This is the trap: precise mode does not make percentiles exact.

questions.scenario: Skewed claim amounts
questions.stem: Insurance claim amounts are heavily right-skewed with a few very large legitimate claims. A data scientist wants to remove only clear data-entry outliers before training a model that predicts claim handling time. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Drop rows outside Q1 − 1.5·IQR and Q3 + 1.5·IQR, computed after a log transform of claim amount
Keep all rows and remove the claim amount column
Drop rows outside mean ± 2 standard deviations of claim amount
Drop the top 10% of claim amounts
questions.explanation: Standard-deviation bounds assume symmetry and are inflated by the very values they should catch, so they behave poorly on heavy skew. Applying the robust IQR rule on log-scaled amounts flags implausible values without discarding the legitimate long tail.
rationales: Correct: a robust rule on a less skewed scale targets true anomalies.
Dropping a likely predictive feature to avoid outliers loses signal.
On skewed data, mean and stddev are distorted and a 2σ cut would discard many legitimate large claims.
An arbitrary percentile cut removes real data regardless of whether it is an error.

questions.scenario: IQR bounds in PySpark
questions.stem: Which PySpark snippet correctly computes the IQR outlier bounds for column "latency_ms"?
options: q1, q3 = df.approxQuantile("latency_ms", [0.25, 0.75], 0.01); lo, hi = q1 - 1.5*(q3-q1), q3 + 1.5*(q3-q1)
lo, hi = df.agg(F.min("latency_ms"), F.max("latency_ms")).first()
q1, q3 = df.approxQuantile("latency_ms", [0.25, 0.75], 0.01); lo, hi = q1 - 3*q1, q3 + 3*q3
m, s = df.agg(F.mean("latency_ms"), F.stddev("latency_ms")).first(); lo, hi = m - 1.5*s, m + 1.5*s
questions.explanation: The IQR rule uses Q1 − 1.5·IQR and Q3 + 1.5·IQR, where IQR = Q3 − Q1, and approxQuantile returns the requested quantiles. The other snippets either scale the wrong quantity, mix in the standard-deviation rule, or keep every row.
rationales: Correct: quartiles from approxQuantile and the 1.5·IQR fences.
Min and max bounds keep every row, so nothing is removed.
Multiplying each quartile by 3 is not the IQR rule.
That is a standard-deviation rule with an unusual k, not the IQR rule.

questions.scenario: Outlier bounds and evaluation
questions.stem: A pipeline computes 3σ bounds on the full dataset, filters outliers, and then splits into train and test. Validation RMSE looks excellent but production error is much higher. Which change best addresses the issue?
options: Increase k from 3 to 5 so fewer rows are removed
Split first, compute bounds on the training set only, and apply the same bounds when scoring
Remove outliers only from the test set
Compute separate bounds on the test set so it is cleaned independently
questions.explanation: Computing bounds on all data before splitting lets test-set statistics shape the training data, and cleaning the test set hides the extreme cases production will see. Fitting the rule on training data and applying it consistently keeps evaluation honest.
rationales: Changing k does not fix the leakage or the mismatch between evaluation and production data.
Correct: fit preprocessing on training data and apply it unchanged downstream.
Cleaning only the test set makes metrics look better without improving the model.
Independent bounds on the test set still use test statistics and make the test set unrepresentative.

questions.scenario: Fraud features
questions.stem: A team building a card-fraud classifier proposes removing all transactions outside 1.5·IQR of amount before training. Fraud makes up 0.3% of rows and is concentrated in unusually large amounts. What is the best response?
options: Switch to the 3σ rule, which removes fewer rows
Drop the amount feature entirely to avoid outliers
Do not drop these rows; extreme amounts carry the fraud signal, so keep them and consider capping or transforming the feature instead
Proceed, because IQR filtering is the standard preprocessing step
questions.explanation: Outlier removal is meant for errors, not for rare but genuine behaviour. In fraud detection the extremes are often the positive class, so dropping them deletes signal; capping or log-transforming limits their leverage while keeping the rows.
rationales: Changing the rule still removes genuine extreme transactions.
Removing a key predictor weakens the model.
Correct: keep signal-bearing extremes and reduce their influence by other means.
Applying a rule blindly would remove a large share of the fraud examples.

A histogram of each column
Pearson correlation between the StringIndexer outputs

rationales: Correct: a contingency table with a chi-square test is the standard comparison.
A scatter plot of codes shows overlapping points on a grid with no meaningful scale.
Separate histograms show each distribution but not the association.
Indexes are arbitrary codes, so a linear correlation on them is meaningless.

questions.scenario: Monotonic but non-linear
questions.stem: Two continuous features show a clear monotonic but strongly curved relationship, with a handful of extreme points. Which statistic best summarises their association?

Mean of each column
Pearson correlation
Spearman rank correlation
questions.explanation: Spearman correlation works on ranks, so it captures monotonic relationships that are not linear and is less affected by extreme values. Pearson measures only linear association and is sensitive to outliers.
rationales: Chi-square tests independence of categorical variables.
Column means say nothing about the relationship between them.
Pearson understates a curved relationship and is pulled by extremes.
Correct: rank-based Spearman suits monotonic, non-linear relationships.

The long tail drags the mean above a typical value.

Replace Imputer with na.drop() on the full dataset

Call randomSplit first, then fit the Imputer (ideally inside a Pipeline) on the training split and transform both splits with the fitted model

The strategy does not change where the statistic is learned from.

options: Missing ages are replaced with the mean of the column
Missing ages are replaced with the median of the column
Missing ages are replaced with the mode of the column
Fitting fails because strategy is required
questions.explanation: The Spark ML Imputer default strategy is "mean". Median and mode must be requested explicitly.
rationales: Correct: mean is the default strategy.
Median is available but not the default.
Mode is available but not the default.
strategy has a default, so fitting succeeds.

questions.scenario: Encoding for logistic regression
questions.stem: A logistic regression model in Spark ML uses a nominal feature region with eight values. The developer runs StringIndexer and feeds region_idx straight into VectorAssembler. What is the main problem?
options: The model will treat the index values as an ordered magnitude, implying relationships between regions that do not exist
StringIndexer output cannot be used by VectorAssembler
StringIndexer sorts categories alphabetically, which breaks the model
Logistic regression cannot use categorical information at all
questions.explanation: A linear model multiplies each input by one coefficient, so an index of 0 to 7 is read as an ordered numeric scale. One-hot encoding after indexing gives each region its own indicator column.
rationales: Correct: index codes impose a false order on a nominal feature.
VectorAssembler accepts numeric columns such as indexes.
By default StringIndexer orders by frequency, and the ordering is not the core issue.
Logistic regression handles categories once they are one-hot encoded.

sources.title: Extracting, transforming and selecting features — Spark MLlib Guide

questions.scenario: High-cardinality feature with trees
questions.stem: A random forest in Spark ML must use a merchant_id feature with about 50,000 distinct values. A teammate proposes one-hot encoding it. Which response is best?
options: Agree, because tree models require one-hot encoded inputs
One-hot encode and then increase the number of trees to compensate
Avoid one-hot encoding here; it creates a huge sparse feature space that weakens tree splits, so group rare merchants or use another encoding such as frequency or target encoding
Convert merchant_id to a float and use it as a continuous feature without further thought
questions.explanation: One-hot encoding a very high-cardinality feature produces tens of thousands of sparse columns, and tree models split on one column at a time, so each split sees little signal and trees grow deep. Grouping rare levels or using frequency or target encoding keeps the information compact.
rationales: Tree models can split on indexed categories directly and do not need OHE.
More trees do not fix the sparsity and dimensionality problem.
Correct: high cardinality is a classic case where OHE is a poor fit.
Treating arbitrary IDs as a continuous scale imposes a meaningless order.

questions.scenario: Ordinal sizes
questions.stem: A feature shirt_size takes values S, M, L and XL. The model is a gradient-boosted tree regressor. Which encoding is most appropriate?
options: Hash into 1,024 buckets
Drop the feature because trees cannot use categories
Map to an ordered integer index (S=0, M=1, L=2, XL=3)
One-hot encode into four columns
questions.explanation: Ordinal features have a natural order that an ordered index preserves, and tree models can split on it directly. One-hot encoding throws away the ordering and adds columns without benefit.
rationales: Hashing four values is unnecessary and loses the order.
Trees can use indexed categorical and ordinal features.
Correct: an ordered index keeps the meaningful order.
OHE discards the order and fragments the feature for a tree model.

questions.scenario: When OHE is a poor fit (Select two.)
questions.stem: In which two situations is one-hot encoding usually a poor choice? (Select two.)
options: A product SKU feature with 30,000 levels
A three-level nominal feature for a k-nearest-neighbours model
A low-cardinality categorical feature for a decision tree model that can split on indexed categories directly
A five-level nominal feature for a linear regression
questions.explanation: One-hot encoding is a poor fit for very high-cardinality features and is usually unnecessary for tree models that split on indexed categories. Low-cardinality nominal features for distance-based or linear models are where OHE fits best.
rationales: Correct: 30,000 levels explode the feature space.
Distance-based models need OHE so codes are not treated as distances.
Correct: trees can split on indexed categories and OHE only fragments them.
Linear models need OHE for nominal features.

questions.scenario: Log-transformed target metrics
questions.stem: A regression model predicts log1p(rent) for apartment listings. The team computes RMSE between the raw model output and the original rent column and reports a value under 1. What should they do?
options: Apply log1p to the predictions again before computing RMSE
Switch to R², which does not need any conversion
Report it; low RMSE means the model is accurate
Apply expm1 to the predictions, then compute RMSE against the original rent values
questions.explanation: The model outputs values in log space, so comparing them with raw rents mixes units and is meaningless. Inverting the transform with expm1 brings predictions back to rent units before computing RMSE or MAE.
rationales: Applying log1p twice moves further from the original scale.
R² on mismatched scales is equally invalid.
The number compares log values with raw rents and is not a valid error.
Correct: invert the transform before computing metrics in original units.

questions.scenario: Which feature to log-transform
questions.stem: Which feature is the best candidate for a log transform before training a linear model?
options: A binary flag indicating premium membership
Daily temperature in Celsius, roughly symmetric and including negative values
Customer satisfaction score on a 1 to 5 scale
Website session counts per user, ranging from 0 to 250,000 with a long right tail
questions.explanation: Log transforms suit positive, right-skewed values that span several orders of magnitude; log1p also handles the zeros. Symmetric, signed, binary or narrow-range features gain nothing and may be undefined under a log.
rationales: A 0/1 flag is not changed in any useful way.
Negative values make the log undefined, and the data is already symmetric.
A narrow ordinal scale is not skewed across orders of magnitude.
Correct: skewed counts with zeros fit log1p well.

questions.scenario: Preparing a linear model (Select two.)
questions.stem: A linear regression will use transaction_amount (positive, highly right-skewed, some zeros) and payment_method (4 nominal values). Which two preprocessing steps are most appropriate? (Select two.)
options: StringIndexer only for payment_method, using the index as a numeric input
StringIndexer followed by OneHotEncoder for payment_method
Apply log to transaction_amount without handling zeros
Apply log1p to transaction_amount
questions.explanation: log1p reduces the skew of a positive feature and stays defined at zero. A linear model needs nominal categories one-hot encoded after indexing so the index is not read as a magnitude.
rationales: A raw index imposes a false order on payment methods.
Correct: indexing then one-hot encoding suits a low-cardinality nominal feature in a linear model.
log(0) is undefined, so rows with zero amounts would fail or become null.
Correct: log1p tames the skew and handles zeros.

questions.scenario: A telecom team must predict next month’s data usage in gigabytes for each subscriber. They have two years of labelled history and want a first model the business can interpret.
questions.stem: Which approach should they try first?
options: A linear regression baseline, then compare tree ensembles on the same validation metric
K-means clustering of subscribers into usage groups
A logistic regression classifier on usage above or below the median
A gradient-boosted classifier with many trees
questions.explanation: Usage in gigabytes is continuous, so this is regression, and an interpretable baseline is the sensible starting point before more complex models. The other options turn the problem into classification or unsupervised learning and discard information.
rationales: Correct. A continuous label needs regression, and a linear baseline gives interpretable coefficients to beat.
Clustering ignores the labels and does not predict a number.
Binarising the target throws away the magnitude the business asked for.
A classifier does not predict a continuous quantity, and it is not the interpretable first step.

sources.title: Classification and regression — Apache Spark MLlib

questions.scenario: A payments company trains a fraud classifier where 0.5% of transactions are fraudulent. The first model reports 99.5% accuracy but flags almost no fraud.
questions.stem: What is the best next step?
options: Remove the fraud rows to make the data cleaner
Keep the model because 99.5% accuracy beats the target
Switch to a regression model on the fraud label
Evaluate with recall, precision or PR AUC and retrain with class weights for the fraud class
questions.explanation: With 0.5% positives, always predicting "not fraud" gives 99.5% accuracy, so accuracy hides the failure. Metrics focused on the positive class plus cost-sensitive training address both the measurement and the model.
rationales: Removing the rare class makes the problem impossible to learn.
The accuracy equals the majority-class rate, so the model has learned nothing useful.
The label is binary; a regression model does not fix the imbalance.
Correct. Positive-class metrics expose the problem and class weights make missed fraud costlier during training.

sources.title: Classification and regression — Apache Spark MLlib

questions.scenario: A data scientist has an imbalanced dataset of 200,000 rows. They oversample the minority class to a 50/50 ratio, then randomly split into 80% training and 20% validation. Validation recall is excellent, but production recall is poor.
questions.stem: What most likely caused the gap?
options: The validation split was too small to compute recall
Oversampling always reduces recall in production
Recall cannot be computed on balanced data
Duplicated minority rows ended up in both training and validation, inflating validation scores
questions.explanation: Oversampling before splitting copies minority rows, so identical rows appear in both splits and validation measures memorisation. Resampling must happen after the split and only on training data.
rationales: 40,000 rows is plenty to compute recall.
Oversampling done correctly on training data often improves recall; the problem is the order of operations.
Recall is defined for any labelled data, balanced or not.
Correct. Resampling before the split leaks copies of training rows into validation.

sources.title: Model selection and tuning — Apache Spark MLlib

questions.stem: Which TWO Spark ML components are Estimators? (Select two.)
options: A fitted LogisticRegressionModel
StringIndexer
VectorAssembler
StandardScaler
questions.explanation: StringIndexer learns the category-to-index mapping and StandardScaler learns column statistics, so both implement fit() and are Estimators. VectorAssembler is a stateless Transformer, and a fitted model is a Transformer.
rationales: Fitted models implement transform(), so they are Transformers.
Correct. It must learn the label mapping from data, so it is an Estimator.
It only concatenates columns into a vector and learns nothing, so it is a Transformer.
Correct. It learns means and standard deviations during fit().

sources.title: Extracting, transforming and selecting features — Apache Spark MLlib

questions.scenario: An engineer defines pipeline = Pipeline(stages=[indexer, assembler, rf]) and calls model = pipeline.fit(train_df).
questions.stem: What type is model, and how should it score new data?
options: An Estimator; call model.evaluate(new_df)
A Pipeline; call model.fit(new_df) again
A RandomForestClassifier; call model.predict(new_df)
A PipelineModel; call model.transform(new_df)
questions.explanation: Pipeline.fit() returns a PipelineModel, which is a Transformer whose stages are all fitted transformers. Scoring is done with transform().
rationales: A PipelineModel is a Transformer, not an Estimator, and has no evaluate() for scoring.
Refitting on new data would retrain instead of scoring.
fit() returns the PipelineModel, not the unfitted classifier, and Spark ML scores DataFrames with transform().
Correct. A PipelineModel is a Transformer and scores with transform().

questions.scenario: A team standardises features with StandardScaler fitted on the full dataset, then splits into training and test sets and tunes a model with CrossValidator on the scaled training data.
questions.stem: What is the most important improvement?
options: Increase numFolds so the leakage averages out
Replace StandardScaler with VectorAssembler
Put StandardScaler and the model in one Pipeline and pass the Pipeline to CrossValidator
Fit StandardScaler on the test set instead
questions.explanation: Fitting the scaler on all data leaks test-set statistics into training. Putting the scaler in a Pipeline used as the CrossValidator estimator refits it on each training fold only.
rationales: More folds do not remove leakage that happened before the split.
VectorAssembler does not scale features, so this removes a needed step.
Correct. A Pipeline estimator refits preprocessing inside each fold and keeps held-out data unseen.
Fitting on the test set is still leakage, just in the other direction.

sources.title: Model selection and tuning — Apache Spark MLlib

questions.stem: In Spark ML, what does an Estimator’s fit() method return?
options: A Model, which is a Transformer
A ParamMap of the best hyperparameters
A new Estimator with updated defaults
A DataFrame with predictions appended
questions.explanation: An Estimator learns from data in fit() and produces a Model. That Model implements transform(), so it is a Transformer.
rationales: Correct. For example, LogisticRegression.fit() returns a LogisticRegressionModel.
ParamMaps configure estimators; fit() does not return one.
fit() produces a fitted model, not another unfitted Estimator.
Appending predictions is what transform() does on a Model.

questions.scenario: A data scientist must tune six hyperparameters of a gradient-boosted model with a budget of 60 training runs. Several hyperparameters are likely unimportant.
questions.stem: Which search strategy is the weakest choice for this budget?
options: Random search over distributions for each hyperparameter
Bayesian search with TPE
Grid search over a few values per hyperparameter
Optuna with its default TPESampler
questions.explanation: With six hyperparameters, even two values each give 64 combinations, so a grid either exceeds the budget or uses very few values and repeats them for unimportant dimensions. Random and Bayesian (TPE) search use the budget far more efficiently.
rationales: Random search explores more distinct values of the important hyperparameters for the same budget.
TPE uses past results to focus the budget on promising regions.
Correct. A grid explodes combinatorially and wastes runs on unimportant hyperparameters.
Optuna’s default TPESampler is a Bayesian method that suits this budget well.

questions.stem: A Hyperopt objective returns the validation AUC as "loss". What will fmin do?
options: Search for the configuration with the highest AUC
Ignore the value and use log loss instead
Search for the configuration with the lowest AUC
Raise an error because AUC must be between 0 and 1
questions.explanation: fmin always minimises the returned loss. To maximise AUC the objective must return its negative (or 1 - AUC).
rationales: This would only happen if the objective returned -AUC.
fmin uses exactly what the objective returns.
Correct. fmin minimises, so returning AUC drives the search toward the worst models.
Hyperopt accepts any scalar loss; there is no range check.

questions.scenario: A team tunes a single-node scikit-learn model on a Databricks cluster with eight workers using Hyperopt on DBR 15.4 LTS ML.
questions.stem: Which configuration trains several candidate models at the same time across the workers?
options: fmin with max_evals=8
fmin with algo=rand.suggest and no trials argument
fmin with the default Trials class
fmin with trials=SparkTrials(parallelism=8)
questions.explanation: SparkTrials distributes trials of single-machine models to Spark workers, running each as a task so many fit at once. The default Trials class runs trials sequentially on the driver.
rationales: max_evals sets the total number of trials, not their parallelism.
The algorithm choice does not change where trials run; without SparkTrials they are sequential.
Trials runs one trial after another on the driver.
Correct. SparkTrials runs single-node trials in parallel on the workers.

questions.scenario: An engineer uses Hyperopt to tune a Spark MLlib GBTClassifier on a large table and wraps the objective in fmin with SparkTrials(parallelism=16). Jobs are slow and fail with resource errors.
questions.stem: What should they change?
options: Use the default Trials class, because MLlib training is already distributed
Raise parallelism to 128 to use more executors
Convert the GBTClassifier to a Pipeline
Switch algo to rand.suggest
questions.explanation: SparkTrials is meant for single-machine models. Distributed algorithms such as MLlib should run under the default Trials class, so each trial uses the cluster instead of competing tasks.
rationales: Correct. Databricks docs say not to use SparkTrials with distributed training such as MLlib.
More parallel trials make the resource contention worse.
Wrapping in a Pipeline does not change how trials are executed.
The search algorithm does not fix running distributed jobs inside Spark tasks.

questions.scenario: A data scientist runs Hyperopt with tpe.suggest, max_evals=40 and SparkTrials(parallelism=40) to finish as fast as possible.
questions.stem: What is the main drawback of this setting?
options: MLflow cannot log more than 10 child runs
Hyperopt will run only one trial per worker in total
All trials start without results from earlier trials, so TPE behaves essentially like random search
SparkTrials does not support tpe.suggest
questions.explanation: TPE improves by using finished trials to choose new ones. When parallelism equals max_evals, every trial is proposed up front, losing the adaptive benefit.
rationales: There is no such MLflow limit; each trial becomes a child run.
Trials are scheduled as tasks; workers can run more than one over the search.
Correct. High parallelism trades adaptivity for speed; keep it well below max_evals.
SparkTrials works with tpe.suggest.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about Hyperopt on Databricks are accurate? (Select two.)
options: Hyperopt is the tuning library Databricks recommends for new projects
When used with MLflow, fmin produces a parent run with child runs per trial
Hyperopt is not included in Databricks Runtime ML after 16.4 LTS ML
SparkTrials is required for Spark MLlib models
questions.explanation: Databricks documents the parent and child run structure for fmin and states that Hyperopt is no longer included after DBR 16.4 LTS ML. It recommends Optuna or Ray Tune for new work, and SparkTrials should not be used with MLlib.
rationales: Databricks now recommends Optuna or Ray Tune because Hyperopt is unmaintained.
Correct. Each trial is logged as a child of the fmin parent run.
Correct. Databricks removed Hyperopt from DBR ML after 16.4 LTS ML.
For MLlib, the default Trials class is the right choice.

questions.scenario: A team on Databricks Runtime 17.3 LTS ML wants to start a new hyperparameter tuning project for an XGBoost model and parallelise trials across the cluster.
questions.stem: Which approach follows current Databricks guidance?
options: AutoML with Standard access mode
A manual Python for-loop over a parameter grid on the driver
Optuna with MlflowStorage and MlflowSparkStudy
Hyperopt with SparkTrials, since it is preinstalled
questions.explanation: Hyperopt is not included after DBR 16.4 LTS ML, and Databricks recommends Optuna, using MlflowSparkStudy with MlflowStorage to run trials in parallel on Spark. A driver loop is sequential and AutoML does not support Standard access mode.
rationales: AutoML does not work on Standard (shared) access mode.
A driver loop does not use the cluster and has no adaptive search.
Correct. This is the documented way to run parallel Optuna studies on Databricks.
Hyperopt is not preinstalled after 16.4 LTS ML and is unmaintained.

questions.stem: In an Optuna objective function, how should a learning rate be sampled across several orders of magnitude, such as 0.0001 to 0.3?
options: trial.suggest_int("lr", 1, 3000)
trial.suggest_float("lr", 1e-4, 0.3) with a uniform scale
trial.suggest_categorical("lr", [0.0001, 0.3])
trial.suggest_float("lr", 1e-4, 0.3, log=True)
questions.explanation: A log-scale float spends equal effort on each order of magnitude, which suits learning rates. Uniform sampling would almost never try the small values.
rationales: An integer range does not represent the continuous learning rate.
Uniform sampling spends most trials near the top of the range.
Only two values ignores everything in between.
Correct. log=True samples evenly across orders of magnitude.

questions.stem: What are Optuna’s default sampler and pruner?
options: CmaEsSampler and SuccessiveHalvingPruner
GridSampler and NopPruner
TPESampler and MedianPruner
RandomSampler and HyperbandPruner
questions.explanation: Optuna's create_study uses the Bayesian TPESampler and MedianPruner when no sampler or pruner is given. Other samplers and pruners exist but must be chosen explicitly.
rationales: CMA-ES and successive halving are optional.
Grid sampling is not the default.
Correct. These are the defaults.
Random sampling and Hyperband are options, not defaults.

questions.scenario: A Spark ML grid has 4 values for maxDepth and 3 values for maxBins. The team uses CrossValidator with numFolds=3.
questions.stem: How many models are trained during the cross-validation search, excluding the final refit on the full dataset?
questions.explanation: The grid has 4 × 3 = 12 combinations, and each is trained once per fold, giving 12 × 3 = 36 models. Including the final refit of the best combination would make 37.
rationales: 37 includes the final refit, which the question excludes.
Adding the grid sizes and folds (4 + 3 + 3) is not how the count works.
12 is the number of combinations, not the number of fits.
Correct. 12 combinations × 3 folds = 36.

questions.scenario: A grid has 5 values of regParam and 2 values of elasticNetParam. The team uses TrainValidationSplit(trainRatio=0.8).
questions.stem: How many models are trained during the search, excluding the final refit?
questions.explanation: TrainValidationSplit evaluates each combination once, so 5 × 2 = 10 models are trained. The final refit on all the data would add one more.
rationales: 8 does not correspond to the grid.
50 would require 5 folds, which TrainValidationSplit does not use.
Correct. 10 combinations × 1 split = 10.
11 includes the final refit, which the question excludes.

questions.scenario: A team has 1.2 billion training rows. Each model takes 40 minutes to train, and the grid has 16 combinations.
questions.stem: Which tuning setup best balances reliability and cost?
options: CrossValidator with numFolds=1
No validation; choose the parameters with the lowest training error
TrainValidationSplit, because with this much data a single split gives a stable estimate at a fraction of the cost
CrossValidator with numFolds=10 to maximise reliability
questions.explanation: With very large data, one validation split already yields a reliable estimate, and TrainValidationSplit trains each combination once instead of k times. Ten-fold CV would multiply an already long run by ten.
rationales: CrossValidator requires at least two folds; one fold is not cross-validation.
Training error does not measure generalisation and favours overfitting.
Correct. Large data plus expensive training favours the cheaper single split.
160 fits of 40 minutes each buys little extra reliability with this much data.

sources.title: Model selection and tuning — Apache Spark MLlib

questions.stem: After CrossValidator finishes its search, which model does cvModel.bestModel contain?
options: An average of the k fold models
The best parameter combination refit on the entire input dataset
The single fold model with the highest metric
The last model trained in the search
questions.explanation: CrossValidator averages metrics across folds to pick the best ParamMap, then refits the estimator with it on the whole dataset. That refit is the bestModel.
rationales: Spark does not average model weights across folds.
Correct. The best ParamMap is refit on all of the data.
Fold models are not returned as the best model.
Training order has nothing to do with which model is returned.

sources.title: Model selection and tuning — Apache Spark MLlib

questions.stem: Which TWO statements correctly compare k-fold cross-validation with a single train-validation split? (Select two.)
options: Cross-validation costs roughly k times more training per combination
Cross-validation gives a more reliable estimate on small datasets
Cross-validation does not require an evaluator
A train-validation split always produces a less biased estimate
questions.explanation: Each combination is trained k times in CV, which costs more but uses every row for validation once, giving a steadier estimate on small data. A single split depends on one random partition, and both tuners need an evaluator.
rationales: Correct. k fits per combination instead of one.
Correct. Averaging over folds reduces the noise of one split.
Both CrossValidator and TrainValidationSplit take an evaluator.
A single split is noisier, not more reliable.

questions.scenario: A team wants CrossValidator to evaluate several parameter combinations at the same time on a large cluster.
questions.stem: Which setting should they change?
options: Wrap the model in SparkTrials
Increase numFolds
Set collectSubModels to True
Set parallelism on CrossValidator to a value such as 4 to 10
questions.explanation: CrossValidator and TrainValidationSplit have a parallelism parameter that evaluates parameter sets in parallel; Spark docs say up to 10 is sufficient for most clusters. The other settings change the amount of work or what is kept, not concurrency.
rationales: SparkTrials belongs to Hyperopt, not Spark ML tuners.
More folds add work rather than running it in parallel.
collectSubModels keeps fold models in memory; it does not add concurrency.
Correct. parallelism controls how many combinations are fit concurrently.

sources.title: Model selection and tuning — Apache Spark MLlib

questions.scenario: An insurer flags claims for manual investigation. Missing a fraudulent claim is very costly, while an extra investigation is cheap.
questions.stem: Which metric should drive model selection?
options: Recall for the fraud class
Precision for the fraud class
Accuracy
R²
questions.explanation: When false negatives are the expensive error, recall on the positive class measures how many fraudulent claims are caught. Precision would favour models that flag fewer claims.
rationales: Correct. Recall rewards catching as many fraud cases as possible.
Precision protects against false positives, which are cheap here.
Accuracy is dominated by the many legitimate claims.
R² is a regression metric.

questions.scenario: A marketing team ranks customers by predicted purchase probability and chooses the cut-off later, depending on campaign budget. Classes are roughly balanced.
questions.stem: Which metric best compares candidate models now?
options: MAE
ROC AUC
Accuracy at a 0.5 threshold
F1 at a 0.5 threshold
questions.explanation: ROC AUC measures ranking quality across all thresholds, which matches a cut-off chosen later. F1 and accuracy depend on one fixed threshold.
rationales: MAE is a regression metric.
Correct. AUC is threshold-independent and evaluates ranking.
Accuracy also fixes the threshold.
F1 judges one threshold the team has not chosen yet.

questions.scenario: A credit team feeds predicted default probabilities into a pricing formula, so a confident wrong probability directly misprices a loan.
questions.stem: Which metric most directly penalises that kind of error?
options: ROC AUC
Accuracy
Log loss
Recall
questions.explanation: Log loss evaluates the predicted probabilities themselves and heavily penalises confident wrong predictions. AUC only measures ranking, and accuracy and recall depend on thresholded labels.
rationales: Two models with very different probabilities can share an AUC if their ranking is the same.
Accuracy ignores how confident each prediction was.
Correct. Log loss rewards calibrated probabilities.
Recall ignores probability values and false positives.

questions.scenario: A model detects a defect that appears in 0.3% of parts. Two candidates have nearly identical ROC AUC, but one finds far more defects at useful precision.
questions.stem: Which metric would better separate them?
options: Area under the precision-recall curve (PR AUC)
Training loss
Accuracy
R²
questions.explanation: With a very rare positive class, ROC AUC is flattered by the many easy true negatives. PR AUC focuses on precision and recall for the positive class and exposes the difference.
rationales: Correct. PR AUC is more informative under heavy imbalance.
Training loss does not measure generalisation or positive-class performance.
Accuracy is around 99.7% for any model that predicts "no defect".
R² is for regression.

questions.scenario: A retailer forecasts daily units per store. Occasional promotions cause huge spikes that are not representative, and the business wants a metric that is not dominated by them.
questions.stem: Which metric fits best?
options: Log loss
RMSE
R²
MAE
questions.explanation: MAE weights every unit of error equally, so a few extreme errors do not dominate it. RMSE squares errors and is pulled strongly by the spikes.
rationales: Log loss is a classification metric.
RMSE penalises large errors heavily, the opposite of what is wanted.
R² is relative to variance and is also driven by squared errors.
Correct. MAE is more robust to outliers.

questions.scenario: A logistics company predicts delivery time. Being very late is far worse than being slightly late, so large errors must be penalised more.
questions.stem: Which metric should guide tuning?
options: F1
MAE
RMSE
Accuracy
questions.explanation: RMSE squares errors before averaging, so large misses count disproportionately. MAE treats all errors linearly.
rationales: F1 is for classification.
MAE does not give extra weight to large errors.
Correct. Squared errors make large misses dominate.
Accuracy is for classification.

questions.stem: A regression model has R² = 0.82 on validation data. What does this mean?
options: 82% of predictions are exactly correct
The model explains about 82% of the variance in the target
The RMSE is 0.18
Predictions are within 18% of the true value on average
questions.explanation: R² is the share of the target’s variance explained by the model relative to predicting the mean. It does not state error size or percentage error.
rationales: R² says nothing about exact matches.
Correct. R² measures variance explained.
R² and RMSE are different quantities in different units.
R² is not a percentage error; use MAE or RMSE for error size.

questions.scenario: A team uses BinaryClassificationEvaluator in a CrossValidator without setting metricName.
questions.stem: Which metric selects the best model?
options: areaUnderPR
areaUnderROC
f1
accuracy
questions.explanation: BinaryClassificationEvaluator defaults to areaUnderROC. To use PR AUC, set metricName to areaUnderPR.
rationales: areaUnderPR must be set explicitly.
Correct. areaUnderROC is the default.
f1 is the default of MulticlassClassificationEvaluator, not the binary evaluator.
accuracy is a MulticlassClassificationEvaluator metric.

sources.title: Model selection and tuning — Apache Spark MLlib

questions.stem: Which TWO are valid metricName values for Spark’s RegressionEvaluator? (Select two.)
options: areaUnderROC
logLoss
mae
r2
questions.explanation: RegressionEvaluator supports rmse (default), mse, mae and r2. logLoss is a multiclass classification metric and areaUnderROC belongs to the binary evaluator.
rationales: areaUnderROC belongs to BinaryClassificationEvaluator.
logLoss belongs to MulticlassClassificationEvaluator.
Correct. Mean absolute error is supported.
Correct. R² is supported.

questions.scenario: A team trains a GBTRegressor on log1p(claim_amount) because claims are heavily right-skewed. They compute RMSE = 0.41 directly on the prediction column and compare it with a model trained on raw claim amounts that has RMSE = 3,900.
questions.stem: What should they do to compare the models fairly?
options: Compare R² only, since it needs no transformation
Pick the log model because 0.41 is smaller than 3,900
Apply log1p to the raw model’s RMSE
Apply expm1 to the log-model predictions and compute RMSE against the original claim_amount
questions.explanation: The log model’s RMSE is in log units, so it is not comparable with an RMSE in currency. Inverting the transform with expm1 and scoring against the original label puts both models on the same scale.
rationales: R² on log scale and on raw scale also differ; the predictions must be back-transformed first.
The two numbers are in different units, so the comparison is meaningless.
Transforming a summary metric does not give a valid comparison.
Correct. Back-transform predictions, then evaluate on the original scale.

questions.scenario: A model trained on log(revenue) produces a prediction column in log space. A stakeholder asks for MAE in dollars.
questions.stem: Which step is required before computing MAE?
options: Exponentiate the predictions with exp() and compare with the original revenue
No step; MAE is scale-invariant
Take the log of the original revenue column and compute MAE in log space
Multiply predictions by the mean revenue
questions.explanation: The model was trained with log, so exp() returns predictions to dollars. MAE then reports the average absolute error in dollars.
rationales: Correct. exp() inverts log so MAE is in dollars.
MAE is expressed in the units of the values it compares, so it is not scale-invariant.
That gives MAE in log units, not dollars.
Scaling by the mean does not invert a log transform.

questions.scenario: A random forest reaches RMSE 2.1 on training data and 9.8 on validation data. Increasing the number of features did not help.
questions.stem: Which TWO actions are most likely to improve validation RMSE? (Select two.)
options: Gather more training data
Evaluate on the training set instead
Increase maxDepth so the trees fit the training data more closely
Reduce maxDepth or raise the minimum instances per node
questions.explanation: A large gap between low training error and high validation error indicates high variance. Limiting tree complexity and adding training data both reduce variance.
rationales: Correct. More data helps the model generalise rather than memorise.
Evaluating on training data hides the problem instead of fixing it.
Deeper trees increase variance and widen the gap.
Correct. Shallower trees or larger leaves reduce overfitting.

questions.scenario: A linear regression has training RMSE 14.2 and validation RMSE 14.6 on a target whose relationships with the features are clearly non-linear.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Add stronger L2 regularisation
Reduce the number of features
Increase model capacity, for example with a tree ensemble or non-linear features
Stop training early
questions.explanation: Similar, high errors on training and validation data point to high bias. More model capacity or better features addresses underfitting, while regularisation and feature removal reduce capacity further.
rationales: Regularisation reduces variance and would worsen underfitting.
Fewer features usually makes underfitting worse.
Correct. Underfitting needs a more expressive model or features.
Early stopping limits fitting, which is the wrong direction here.

questions.stem: As model complexity increases, how do training and validation error typically behave?
options: Training error rises while validation error falls
Training error keeps falling, while validation error falls and then rises
Both errors rise steadily
Both errors fall steadily
questions.explanation: More complexity lets the model fit training data ever better, but past a point it fits noise and validation error rises. The best complexity is where validation error is lowest.
rationales: Training error does not rise with added capacity.
Correct. This U-shaped validation curve is the bias-variance trade-off.
Training error falls with complexity.
Validation error eventually rises as the model overfits.
