questions.scenario: An insurer re-prices every active policy once a week. A gradient-boosted model registered in Unity Catalog scores about 40 million policy rows, and the results are written to a Delta table that the pricing team reads on Monday morning. Nobody waits on individual predictions.
questions.stem: Which serving approach fits best?
options: A scheduled job that applies the model with mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf and writes the scores to a Delta table
A Model Serving endpoint called once per policy from a notebook loop
A continuously running Lakeflow pipeline that rescores policies as soon as any row changes
Publishing the policy table to an Online Feature Store and calling an endpoint for each policy
questions.explanation: With a weekly schedule and no one waiting on single predictions, batch inference is the simplest and cheapest choice. A Spark UDF built from the MLflow model scores the table in parallel on the executors. Real-time endpoints and continuous streaming add cost and complexity the requirement does not need.
rationales: Correct: scheduled batch scoring with a Spark UDF matches a weekly whole-table requirement.
Calling a real-time endpoint row by row for 40 million rows is slow and costly; endpoints are for request/response latency.
A continuous pipeline is for data that arrives all the time; the requirement is a weekly repricing.
Online stores and endpoints serve low-latency lookups, which nobody needs here.

questions.scenario: A retailer's mobile app shows "complete your basket" suggestions. The suggestions depend on the items in the shopper's current basket, so they cannot be computed ahead of time, and the app waits for the answer before rendering the page.
questions.stem: How should the team serve the recommendation model?
options: Precompute suggestions for every shopper in an hourly batch job
Deploy the model to a Model Serving endpoint and call its REST API on each page load
Write basket events to a table and score them with a streaming Lakeflow pipeline
Load the model with mlflow.pyfunc.load_model inside a nightly notebook
questions.explanation: The app blocks on the prediction and the input exists only at request time, which is the definition of real-time serving. Model Serving exposes the model as a low-latency REST API on autoscaling compute. Batch and streaming write results to tables for later use and cannot answer a live request.
rationales: Batch precomputation cannot know the current basket.
Correct: a Model Serving endpoint returns a prediction per request with low latency.
A streaming pipeline writes results to a table; the app would still have no synchronous answer.
A nightly notebook is batch and cannot respond to live page loads.

questions.scenario: A manufacturer lands vibration and temperature readings from thousands of machines into a Delta table continuously. Maintenance dashboards must show an anomaly score for each reading within a few minutes. The team wants declarative code with managed checkpoints and autoscaling, and the anomaly model is registered in Unity Catalog.
questions.stem: Which design meets these requirements?
options: A Lakeflow pipeline with an @dp.table that reads the readings with spark.readStream and adds a column from mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf
A notebook that loops forever, converts new rows with toPandas() and calls model.predict()
A Model Serving endpoint that each machine calls before writing its reading
A materialized view that is fully recomputed once a night with the model
questions.explanation: Continuous arrival with minute-level latency and results consumed from tables points to streaming inference. In a Lakeflow pipeline (formerly DLT) you load the model as a Spark UDF and apply it in a streaming table, and the pipeline manages checkpoints and autoscaling. The other options either do not scale, change the producers, or miss the latency target.
rationales: Correct: a streaming table applying a spark_udf is the documented streaming-inference pattern, and the pipeline provides managed autoscaling.
A driver-side pandas loop has no checkpointing and does not scale to thousands of machines.
Real-time endpoints add per-request calls the dashboard does not need and require changing every producer.
A nightly recompute misses the few-minutes requirement.

questions.scenario: A data scientist has a 20,000-row pandas DataFrame in a notebook and wants predictions from the version of main.ml.claims_risk that currently holds the Champion alias in Unity Catalog.
questions.stem: Which code returns the predictions?
options: mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("models:/main.ml.claims_risk/Production").predict(pdf)
mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("models:/main.ml.claims_risk@Champion").predict(pdf)
mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf(spark, "models:/main.ml.claims_risk@Champion").predict(pdf)
mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("models:/main.ml.claims_risk@Champion").transform(pdf)
questions.explanation: Unity Catalog models are loaded by alias with the models:/catalog.schema.model@alias URI, and every PyFunc model accepts a pandas DataFrame in predict(). UC does not support stages, so a stage URI fails. A Spark UDF is applied to Spark columns, not called with predict on pandas.
rationales: Unity Catalog does not support stages such as Production; use an alias.
Correct: load by alias and call predict on the pandas DataFrame.
spark_udf returns a UDF for Spark DataFrame columns; it has no predict method for pandas input.
PyFunc models expose predict(), not transform().

questions.scenario: A team must score a 2-billion-row Delta table with a scikit-learn model registered in Unity Catalog. Their first attempt called df.toPandas() and then model.predict(), and the driver ran out of memory.
questions.stem: What should they change?
options: Increase the driver size until toPandas() succeeds
Use collect() and call predict() on each row in a Python loop
Create a UDF with mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf and apply it with df.withColumn so executors score in parallel
Call model.predict(df) directly on the Spark DataFrame
questions.explanation: mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf wraps the model so that each executor scores its own partitions, which avoids pulling the table onto the driver. toPandas() and collect() both move all data to the driver. Calling predict() on a model loaded with load_model runs on the driver as well, so it does not distribute scoring across the cluster.
rationales: A bigger driver only postpones the problem and wastes the cluster's executors.
collect() still moves every row to the driver and is far slower.
Correct: a Spark UDF distributes inference across the cluster.
A model loaded with load_model scores on the driver; even where a Spark DataFrame is accepted it is converted to pandas there, so it does not distribute the work. Use spark_udf for Spark DataFrames.

questions.scenario: A churn model was trained with FeatureLookup objects against two Unity Catalog feature tables and logged with fe.log_model. The monthly scoring input contains only customer_id and the scoring date.
questions.stem: What is the simplest way to batch-score this input with the correct features?
options: mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(uri).predict(input_df.toPandas())
fe.score_batch(model_uri=uri, df=input_df)
mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf(spark, uri) applied to customer_id only
Rebuild the training set with fe.create_training_set and call training_set.load_df() on the scoring input
questions.explanation: A model logged with FeatureEngineeringClient.log_model carries its feature lookup metadata, and fe.score_batch uses it to look up the needed features from the feature tables. The input only needs the lookup keys. Plain pyfunc loading does not perform the lookups, so the model would receive only the IDs.
rationales: Plain pyfunc loading does not look up features, so the model gets only IDs.
Correct: score_batch looks up the features automatically from the packaged metadata.
A plain Spark UDF also lacks the feature lookups.
create_training_set joins features onto a DataFrame to build training data; it does not apply the model, so it is not the scoring API.

questions.scenario: A developer is writing a client for a custom model endpoint. The model expects six named columns, and an earlier prototype produced wrong predictions because columns arrived in a different order.
questions.stem: Which request body format should the client use?
options: dataframe_records
dataframe_split
instances
inputs
questions.explanation: Databricks recommends dataframe_split, which sends the column names separately from row data and preserves column order. dataframe_records does not guarantee column order. instances and inputs are tensor formats for tensor-based models.
rationales: dataframe_records does not guarantee column order, which caused the original bug.
Correct: dataframe_split is the recommended format and preserves column order.
instances is a row-based tensor format, not a named-column DataFrame format.
inputs is a columnar tensor format, not a named-column DataFrame format.

questions.scenario: An endpoint named claims-risk serves a champion version and a challenger version with a 95/5 traffic split. A partner application must get predictions and be part of the A/B test.
questions.stem: Which request should the partner application send?
options: POST /serving-endpoints/claims-risk/invocations
POST /serving-endpoints/claims-risk/served-models/challenger/invocations
POST /api/2.0/serving-endpoints with the input rows in the body
GET /serving-endpoints/claims-risk/invocations with the inputs as query parameters
questions.explanation: Requests to the endpoint's /invocations URL are routed according to the traffic configuration, so the partner takes part in the 95/5 split. The served-models URL targets one model and bypasses the split. POST /api/2.0/serving-endpoints creates endpoints rather than scoring them.
rationales: Correct: the endpoint invocation URL follows the traffic split.
The served-models URL sends every request to the challenger and bypasses the split.
That API creates an endpoint; it does not return predictions.
Scoring requests are POSTs with a JSON body.

questions.scenario: Version 3 of main.ml.claims_risk is serving all traffic on an endpoint. The team has registered version 4 and wants 10% of live traffic to go to it while client applications keep the same URL.
questions.stem: What should they do?
options: Create a second endpoint for version 4 and ask client teams to send every tenth request to it
Transition version 4 to the Staging stage so the endpoint sends it a share of traffic
Add version 4 as a second served entity and set traffic_config routes to 90 and 10 by updating the endpoint configuration
Set a model version tag traffic=10 on version 4
questions.explanation: An endpoint can serve several entities, and traffic_config.routes assigns each a traffic_percentage. Updating the configuration (PUT .../config or Edit configuration in the UI) keeps the same invocation URL for clients. Unity Catalog has no stages, and tags are metadata that do not route requests.
rationales: Splitting in client code is fragile and needs every client to change; the endpoint can split traffic itself.
Unity Catalog does not support stages, and stages never controlled endpoint routing.
Correct: two served entities with traffic_config routes give a 90/10 split behind one URL.
Tags are metadata; they do not affect how an endpoint routes traffic.

questions.scenario: A team wants to serve a custom model that standardises inputs and maps raw scores to risk bands before returning a result. The model will live in Unity Catalog and be served from a Model Serving endpoint.
questions.stem: Which two steps are required? (Select two.)
options: Log a mlflow.pyfunc.PythonModel subclass that implements predict, with an input_example so a signature is recorded
Register the model in Unity Catalog and create an endpoint whose served entity names the model and a version
Transition the model version to the Production stage
Convert the model to ONNX before registering it
questions.explanation: Custom pre- and postprocessing is packaged as a PythonModel with a predict method, and Unity Catalog requires new model versions to have a signature, which an input_example provides. The endpoint then serves a specific UC model version. Stages do not exist in UC, and Model Serving accepts MLflow-format Python models without ONNX conversion.
rationales: Correct: a PythonModel wraps custom logic, and UC model versions must have a signature.
Correct: the served entity references the UC model name and version.
Unity Catalog does not support stages.
Model Serving serves MLflow-format Python models; ONNX conversion is not required.

questions.scenario: An analyst works in SQL and a data engineer works in Python notebooks. Both need predictions from an existing custom model serving endpoint without writing raw HTTP calls.
questions.stem: Which two methods query the endpoint? (Select two.)
options: mlflow.deployments.get_deploy_client("databricks").predict(endpoint=..., inputs=...)
The ai_query SQL function with the endpoint name
fe.score_batch with the endpoint name as model_uri
mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("serving-endpoints/<name>")
questions.explanation: The Databricks docs list the MLflow deployments client and the ai_query SQL function as ways to query a serving endpoint, alongside REST and the Serving UI. fe.score_batch takes a model URI and scores locally on the cluster. pyfunc.load_model loads a model from a model URI, not from an endpoint.
rationales: Correct: the MLflow deployments client queries Databricks serving endpoints from Python.
Correct: ai_query calls a serving endpoint from SQL.
score_batch takes a registered model URI, not an endpoint.
load_model loads model artifacts by model URI; it does not call an endpoint.

sources.title: Query custom model endpoints — Databricks docs

questions.scenario: A real-time pricing model was trained with features from a Unity Catalog feature table and logged with fe.log_model. Client applications know only the product_id when they call the endpoint, and the features must be fetched with low latency.
questions.stem: What should the team do so the endpoint can score requests that contain only product_id?
options: Have every client compute all features and send them in the request
Publish the feature table to a Databricks Online Feature Store; Model Serving then looks up the features from the key
Create a legacy online table from the feature table
Point the endpoint at the offline Delta feature table and let it run a Spark query per request
questions.explanation: The offline Delta feature table is for training and batch scoring, while an Online Feature Store holds a low-latency copy for real-time serving. Once the table is published, Model Serving looks up the features automatically for a model logged with fe.log_model. Legacy online tables are retired.
rationales: This duplicates feature logic in every client and risks training-serving skew.
Correct: published online features are looked up automatically by Model Serving.
Legacy online tables are retired; Online Feature Stores replace them.
The offline table is meant for training and batch scoring, not low-latency per-request lookups.

questions.scenario: A backend service will call a Model Serving endpoint around the clock in production. During the prototype it used a personal access token copied from a data scientist's account.
questions.stem: What does Databricks recommend for authenticating the production service?
options: Keep the data scientist's personal access token and rotate it yearly
OAuth machine-to-machine authentication with a service principal
Make the endpoint public so that no token is needed
Store the workspace admin's password in the service configuration
questions.explanation: Databricks recommends OAuth machine-to-machine (M2M) authentication for production calls to serving endpoints, using a service principal rather than a person. Route-optimised endpoints accept only OAuth. Personal tokens tie production to one person's account.
rationales: Personal tokens tie production to an individual and are not the recommended production method.
Correct: OAuth M2M with a service principal is the recommended production option.
Endpoints require authentication with a Databricks token.
Sharing human credentials is insecure and is not a supported pattern.

questions.scenario: A team has a working pipeline written with import dlt and @dlt.table that applies a model to a stream. They read that Delta Live Tables is now called Lakeflow pipelines.
questions.stem: What must they do to keep the pipeline running?
options: Rewrite it with from pyspark import pipelines as dp before the next run
Nothing; legacy dlt code still works, and the dp module is the current style for new code
Move the model scoring into a Model Serving endpoint, since pipelines no longer support UDFs
Convert every streaming table into a materialized view
questions.explanation: The docs state that existing code using import dlt keeps working and no migration is required. New code can use from pyspark import pipelines as dp with @dp.table. Model UDFs in pipeline tables remain the pattern for streaming inference.
rationales: A rewrite is optional, not required.
Correct: legacy syntax continues to work without migration.
Pipelines still run Spark UDFs such as mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf.
Streaming tables are still supported; materialized views serve a different purpose.

questions.scenario: A card issuer has two fraud requirements: (1) decline a suspicious payment before authorisation completes, and (2) give investigators a table of flagged events, updated within a few minutes, for later review.
questions.stem: Which serving modes best match requirements (1) and (2)?
options: (1) batch, (2) real-time
(1) real-time, (2) streaming
(1) streaming, (2) batch
(1) real-time, (2) real-time
questions.explanation: Declining a payment before authorisation means the system waits on each prediction, which needs a real-time endpoint. A table of flags refreshed within minutes from continuously arriving events is streaming inference. Calling an endpoint for the investigator table would add per-request cost without benefit.
rationales: Batch cannot answer before authorisation, and the investigator table does not need request/response.
Correct: blocking decisions need real-time serving; a minutes-fresh table fits streaming.
Streaming writes results after the fact and cannot block a payment in flight.
The investigator table is consumed from a table, so a streaming pipeline is simpler and cheaper than per-event endpoint calls.
